articles.summary: Trump eases tariffs on Canadian imports weeks before US midterms, offering relief to Maine  The Times of IndiaUS lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods before midterm elections  BBCTrump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms  The HinduTrump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, as Senator Collins faces close race  ReutersUS expected to lift 50% tariffs on select Canadian agricultural imports, WSJ says  Investing.com India
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has eased some tariffs on Canadian imports, with the move coming just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections. The decision could benefit Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is facing a tough re-election contest in Maine, a state whose economy has been affected by the trade dispute with Canada.
The White House said the changes would remove tariffs on certain products, including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment". However, the administration will also introduce tariffs on other goods, including carpets, certain valves and waste products. The new measures will take effect on October 30.
Collins said she had "secured" the exemptions for products important to Maine's agricultural sector, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.
Collins seeks relief for Maine businesses
Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democratic candidate, said farmers in her state depend on supplies from Canada that are difficult or expensive to source elsewhere.
She said many farmers "rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
The senator's intervention comes as Democrats target her seat in their bid to take control of Congress from Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections. 
Maine shares a border with Canada, and businesses in the state have felt the effects of Trump's trade policies.
The partial tariff relief could ease costs for some businesses, although the introduction of duties on other Canadian products means the changes will not benefit every sector.

After renaming Lake Ontario, Google CEO rejects US request to rename Atlantic Ocean
Trade tensions strain US-Canada ties
The United States and Canada have closely connected economies, with roughly 70 per cent of Canadian exports going to the US. Trade relations have deteriorated since negotiations between the two countries broke down in August, prompting Trump to impose a fresh round of tariffs.
Earlier US duties on Canadian cars, steel, aluminium and lumber have hurt businesses, contributed to job losses and weighed on economic growth. Canada entered a technical recession this year after its economy contracted for two consecutive quarters.
The tariffs imposed after the collapse of trade talks affected goods worth around $20 billion, equivalent to 5.5 per cent of Canadian exports to the US. The targeted products ranged from hockey sticks to cement.
Since returning to office for his second term, Trump has imposed extensive tariffs on imports from both allies and rivals, arguing that other countries have taken advantage of the United States.
His administration has also linked some threatened tariffs to broader political and foreign policy goals.

articles.title: India-UK Scotch Whisky Tariff Dispute Raises Trade Pact Concerns - Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.summary: India-UK Scotch Whisky Tariff Dispute Raises Trade Pact Concerns  Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.full_text:
Overview and Implications of the Tariff Dispute
By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 23 (Reuters) - India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.
Background: Negotiations and Agreement Details
Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years.
The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.
Investigation and Industry Response
India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate.
In a letter to the commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI) wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom."
"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond.
Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment, and Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation.
Big Implications for India's Drinks Sector
Impact on Foreign Investors
Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back-tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen.
Pernod's Ongoing Legal Challenges
Pernod is already facing antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing.
Market Impact and Industry Concerns
ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75% of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings.
Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75% tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150% duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s.
Calls for Clarification and Resolution
The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. And ISWAI said in its letter that the India–UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines.
An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants," the letter said.
Official Responses and Next Steps
A spokesperson for the British government said: "We are working with the Government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal."
(Reporting by Aditya Kalra; Additional reporting by Shivangi Acharya and Alistair Smout; Editing by Joe Bavier)

articles.summary: India’s liquor trade group asks government to clarify Scotch tariffs under U.K. trade deal  Vinetur
articles.full_text:
Investigators told importers that bulk Scotch concentrates may still face a 150% duty, alarming Pernod Ricard and Diageo
Friday, October 23, 2026
A trade group representing major liquor companies in India has asked the government for urgent intervention after Indian investigators told importers that reduced tariffs under the new India-United Kingdom trade deal do not apply to bulk shipments of Scotch whisky concentrates, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.
The dispute centers on one of the most closely watched parts of the trade agreement, which took effect on July 15 after years of negotiations. Under the pact, India agreed to cut import duties on certain Scotch whisky products from 150% to 75% immediately, with the rate set to fall to 40% over 10 years. The British government had said the deal would help flagship U.K. products such as whisky.
But Indian tax investigators have privately told companies that bulk imports of Scotch whisky concentrate should not receive the lower 75% duty and instead must be classified under a customs category that attracts the full 150% tariff, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. That position has raised the first major dispute over implementation of the free trade deal and has alarmed companies that rely on imported Scotch spirit for products made and sold in India.
In a letter sent on Friday to India’s commerce minister, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India said the classification issue threatens to undermine a key market access benefit that India and Britain negotiated and agreed under the pact. The group said the preferential tariff treatment could effectively become unavailable for those imports if the current interpretation is maintained.
The association did not comment on the contents of the letter. India’s commerce ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The issue has become more sensitive after India’s Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod Ricard and Diageo this month and questioned executives as part of an investigation into whether the companies wrongly classified imported products in order to claim the lower tariff rate. Earlier this week, both companies told Reuters they were cooperating with Indian authorities.
Pernod declined to comment further. Diageo did not respond to a request for comment.
The case matters because India is one of the world’s largest alcoholic drinks markets and a crucial growth engine for global spirits companies. The country’s liquor market is worth about $65 billion, and imported spirits remain a small but influential part of the business. According to Crisil Ratings, Britain accounts for nearly 75% of spirits imported into India, driven mainly by Scotch whisky.
For companies such as Pernod and Diageo, the tariff interpretation has commercial importance beyond imported premium bottles sold directly to consumers. Both groups import bulk Scotch concentrates and use them in India to make widely sold brands including Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell’s. Industry executives say the economics of those products depend heavily on whether the imported spirit qualifies for the lower duty.
People familiar with the matter said the companies believe the goods shipped from the U.K. should fall under the tariff lines covered by the trade agreement and should therefore receive the reduced 75% duty. The industry association made the same argument in its letter, saying the agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant customs lines.
The group also warned that uncertainty over classification is already affecting business planning and could disrupt legitimate industry operations unless the government issues a clarification quickly. It said prompt action would help ensure that the market access gains negotiated by India and Britain are actually delivered in practice.
A spokesperson for the British government said London is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue and to make sure British companies can export under the tariff terms set out in the trade deal.
The disagreement comes against a broader backdrop of tension between foreign companies and Indian authorities over import classifications and tax demands. Such disputes have long been a source of concern for overseas investors in India, who have in past years faced large claims for back taxes and penalties. Multinational companies including Samsung and Volkswagen have also been caught in customs and tax fights with the Indian government.
Pernod in particular is already under pressure in India on several fronts. The company, whose largest market by volume is India, is facing antitrust cases and a $314 million tax claim from Indian authorities, who have accused it of undervaluing some imports. Pernod has denied any wrongdoing.
The tariff fight over Scotch is politically sensitive as well because whisky was one of the most difficult issues during the India-U.K. trade talks. India has long maintained some of the highest import duties in the world on alcoholic beverages, and Scotch producers had pressed hard for cuts to improve access to a market with rising incomes and strong demand for premium spirits. The final deal was presented by both governments as a breakthrough, with lower tariffs seen as a concrete commercial win for British exporters.
The current dispute suggests that even after a trade agreement takes effect, the commercial outcome can depend on how customs authorities interpret product categories at the border. In this case, the disagreement is not over whether tariff cuts were negotiated, but over which forms of Scotch whisky are entitled to benefit from them.
That question is especially important for India’s domestic spirits industry because bulk Scotch imports are used as inputs in blended products made inside the country. If those imports remain subject to 150% duties, companies may face higher costs, altered sourcing decisions and pressure on margins in a market where competition is intense. Industry officials say it could also weaken one of the practical benefits that the trade agreement was expected to deliver.
So far, Indian authorities have not publicly explained why bulk Scotch concentrate should be excluded from the lower tariff bracket, and there has been no official clarification from the government on how the relevant customs lines should be interpreted under the trade pact. Until that changes, producers and importers are left facing uncertainty over both future shipments and the potential tax exposure tied to past imports now under investigation.
For Pernod and Diageo, the matter carries both legal and financial risk. Investigators are examining whether the companies’ use of the lower rate was proper, and the answer could determine whether they face additional duty demands. For the wider industry, the case has become a test of whether one of the headline promises of the India-U.K. agreement will hold once it reaches the customs gate.

Piyush Goyal says India-EU FTA could be operational in 4-5 months, urging Indian and German businesses to prepare for trade opportunities.
Berlin: Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday expressed confidence that the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) would move rapidly towards signing and could become operational within the next four to five months, urging Indian and German businesses to begin preparations to maximise its benefits.
Addressing an India-Germany business roundtable here, Goyal said companies should start identifying potential customers and collaborators, exchanging product samples and quality requirements, and discussing pricing rather than wait for the agreement to come into force.
“This is the time we need to see businesses start probably doing sampling, exchanging notes of quality required, exchanging pricing, get everything in order so that when the trade agreement comes into effect, we be the first off the block, get the maximum advantage of this agreement,” he said.
The minister said the agreement, finalised earlier this year, would move towards signing quickly, expressing confidence that it could be signed before the end of the calendar year, subject to the requisite procedures.

“You rightly mentioned Ms. von der Leyen’s comment about India and EU FTA being the mother of all deals. It took twenty years, but I can assure you the agreement really got finalised in the last thirteen months,” Goyal said.
He said the conclusion of negotiations had been announced on January 27 and credited the commitment of India and the 27-nation European Union to completing the negotiations.

Goyal said the agreement’s implementation would open up opportunities for businesses, but stressed that companies needed to establish commercial partnerships and prepare their operations in advance to take full advantage of the new framework.
The minister also invited German businesses to explore opportunities in India, highlighting the potential for closer cooperation in manufacturing, investment, technology and skill development.
He said Germany’s technical expertise and industrial capabilities complemented India’s infrastructure expansion, digital strengths and skilled workforce, creating opportunities for both countries to enhance their competitiveness.
Goyal also called for stronger cooperation to improve supply-chain resilience amid global uncertainty, saying India and Germany could work together without compromising economic openness.
He identified economic security, the green transition and emerging technologies as key areas requiring closer collaboration, stressing that trust would remain central to commercial engagement.
The minister said the India-Germany partnership had received fresh impetus under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, including through cooperation in artificial intelligence and semiconductors.
Goyal also acknowledged the role of European Union Trade Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis and other EU trade ministers in advancing the negotiations. He said businesses should now focus on translating the agreement into tangible economic outcomes by connecting trade with investment, manufacturing with research, and industries with academic institutions.
The minister was speaking at an India-Germany business roundtable and inaugurated the India Center at the German Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, aimed at deepening bilateral engagement and strengthening cooperation between stakeholders in the two countries.

articles.title: EU-India FTA: Unpacking Indian food processing sector - Media India Group
articles.summary: EU-India FTA: Unpacking Indian food processing sector  Media India Group
articles.full_text:
After nearly 18 years of protracted negotiations, India and European Union in January this year concluded the landmark Free Trade Agreement (FTA) in New Delhi. The FTA is set to transform India’s trade and economic relations with 27 European Union countries.
On paper, the Indian food processing industry is going to be one of the biggest beneficiaries of the FTA. This is supposed to come through easing market entry and eliminating steep tariffs on value-added goods. India stands at a pivotal moment in its agri-food journey and as one of the world’s largest producers of food grains, fruits, vegetables and dairy, the country has immense potential to lead the global food market.
The FTA seeks to reshape the EU–India trade through more predictable regulatory procedures, improved market-access provisions and deeper supply-chain linkages. While lower tariffs will reduce transaction costs, additional provisions will lower compliance burdens and create new commercial opportunities for Indian food processing sector.
The landmark FTA comes at a critical time for both economies, offering an opportunity to deepen economic cooperation amid growing global uncertainty and disrupted global food supply chain. By reducing barriers across goods and services, the agreement can help the EU diversify its partnerships and strengthen its presence in one of the world’s fastest-growing markets, while enabling India to expand exports, attract investment, upgrade industries and integrate more deeply into global value chains.
The demand for Indian food products in Europe is growing at roughly 10 pc annually, moving far beyond traditional ethnic grocery niches into broader consumer markets. Demand is shifting past traditional Indian diaspora hubs into mainstream European households. Indian food has in fact emerged as a soft power influencing and enhancing European households and lifestyle.
Top items in Indian exports, besides the traditional rice, lentils and spices, dehydrated onion and garlic, are superfoods like makhana and millet-based products and private-label processed foods. The Netherlands has so far been the primary entry point and major destination for EU-bound Indian agricultural and fishery goods, but with the agreement coming into force early next year, all EU countries will be connected directly with the Indian exporters.
For last two decades India’s food processing industry has undergone a profound structural transformation, anchored in a strong agricultural base, a rapidly expanding consumer market and sustained policy support by the government. Once viewed primarily as a supplier of raw agricultural commodities, India has emerged as a reliable global source of value-added food products and modern logistics solutions. This paradigm shift also presents compelling opportunities for European investors seeking scale, resilience, and long-term value in a high-growth emerging Indian food processing sector.
India is uniquely positioned to lead the next phase of global agri-food transformation. With one of the largest and most diverse agricultural ecosystems in the world, India ranks as one of the top producers across a wide spectrum of commodities, including fruits and vegetables, dairy, cereals, millets, pulses, livestock, fisheries, tea, and spices. This abundance of raw material provides a robust platform for processing, value addition and supply chain optimisation.
Regulatory hurdles and compliance
However, if India’s processed food producers think that the FTA has opened the doors to easy fortune for them, they are living in an illusion. They must know that European market is very regulated and is highly standardised. Key challenges and EU regulatory hurdles including safety standards, will remain a challenge for India. Strict Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) measures often lead to cargo rejections or delays. Navigating multi-layered EU certifications and testing standards is expensive and slow.
The EU has very stringent, science-based standards to protect human, animal and plant health. All products imported from India under the agreement will have to respect these standards. The EU will conduct Impact Assessments to analyse potential alignment of production standards between domestic and imported products, notably on pesticides and animal welfare. It will also increase the number of food safety audits reinforcing measures to strengthen EU border controls on imported food, animal and plant products.
Already, Indian exporters frequently face EU border rejections due to stringent Sanitary and Phytosanitary regulations, pesticide residue limits, such as tricyclazole or ethylene oxide and traceability requirements. While exports of grain and dairy processing are robust, fruit and vegetable processing penetration remains low, of under 5 pc, limiting processed exports like juices or ready meals compared to regional competitors.
Not a pandora’s box, a measured market access
The FTA has reduced or zeroed out duties on key value-added items, organic inputs, and processed marine products. But a large share of Indian exports is raw or semi-processed commodities rather than high-margin finished goods.
Under the FTA, the EU has also protected its most sensitive agricultural sectors. Official summaries confirm that products such as beef, chicken meat, rice, sugar, and other politically sensitive farm goods have been excluded from liberalisation under the FTA.
The agreed framework of the FTA is a deliberate political and trade balance and not a blanket free trade. For businesses, while the agreement offers clearer rules and phased access, for governments, it preserves policy space to manage domestic priorities.
Indian exporters will, however, have to face a plethora of challenges, despite imports from the EU of several considerable quantum elements from India. The most notable are non-pricing obstacles such as strict limits on pesticide residues called the Maximum Residue Limits (MRL), health and phytosanitary standards, traceability and hygiene. Other problems, such as the limited acceptance and recognition of Indian certification organisations, add to the cost and the burden of compliance affecting the overall competitiveness of exporters.
Navigating EU’s green wall
Another point of concern for Indian exporters would be that the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) remains fully in force. The CABM imposes tax on import of products that are produced by industries that are carbon intensive, such as steel, aluminium, cement and fertilisers. What this means, in practice, is that if the carbon emissions are not reduced on production in India, then Indian products would be priced higher in the European market because of the imposition of taxes, leading to a major hit to Indian exports.
A critical question for Indian policymakers and exporters is whether the FTA will provide additional leverage to India or whether India will be subjected to the same stringent carbon costs as the other global trading partners. Therefore, without rapid decarbonisation, Indian products are at a risk of being priced out of the European market.
There is a comprehensive work plan with separate provisions under the EU-India free trade agreement to address concerns over the European Union’s carbon tax, and it is hoped that Indian Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) will not face any problems due to that measure. As India is also developing its own carbon pricing mechanism.
The CBAM does not directly target processed food items, but it indirectly increases operational and packaging costs for India’s food processing industry through the supply chain. As food processing relies heavily on metal cans, tinplate, aluminium foils, and machinery components, the packaging cost inflation will come as indirect supply chain pressure. Direct food items are not in the initial CBAM phase, but energy-intensive packaging, fertilisers, and cold-chain logistics face future indirect cost pressures. Moreover, SMEs will face complex emission-tracking and verification demands.
Mainstream and niche consumer demands
India’s agricultural exports to the EU reached EUR 3.8 billion in 2025, establishing the country as the EU’s fifth-largest food and agri-commodity supplier by value, but a large share of that caters to the Indian diaspora, which itself has grown significantly in the last decade or so. Historically, the EU has accounted for about 12 pc of India’s total processed food exports, which translates to about EUR 1 billion or USD 1.15 billion.
Also Read: EU-India FTA: Redefining India’s trade policy for new global era
To make real gains from the FTA, the Indian exporters will need to expand beyond the diaspora market. They will have to move past traditional ethnic grocery stores by introducing authentic Indian flavours, spices, tea, and ready-to-eat meals to mainstream European supermarket chains. They must focus on health and convenience too. They will need to promote organic lines, healthy snacks, and convenient packaged foods that match fast-paced European lifestyles.
Data shows that 1.8 pc of Indian agricultural consignments entering Europe were subject to border rejection or enhanced checks in 2025, primarily due to pesticide residues, which accounted for 41pc of rejections, aflatoxin levels in spices, that caused 28 pc of rejections and documentation non-compliance which made for 31 pc of rejections.
Buyers working directly with unvetted spot-market suppliers face material risk of rejected shipments, demurrage costs, and inventory write-downs. The problem with Indian exporters is that in their rush to make ‘quick money’ in the European market, they tend to forget that once they are blacklisted after repeated alerts, their future in EU market will be fully terminated.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has acknowledged that stability along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) remains intermittent, attributing periodic disturbances to Chinese forces deviating from established patrolling patterns. This admission comes amid a growing disconnect between the government's diplomatic narrative of a "thaw" in relations and the operational realities reported by security forces on the ground.
The MEA's stance follows critical disclosures by the Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), Shatrujeet Kapur. Speaking at an ITBP base in Alwar, Rajasthan, DG Kapur confirmed that confrontations with Chinese troops persist across several sites along the Arunachal Pradesh border. His assessment suggests a shift in the nature of the conflict, asserting that conventional warfare is no longer sufficient to counter China's tactics. In response, the ITBP has integrated drone platoons into all border units and introduced a specialized 'Strike' course designed to manage high-intensity skirmishes similar to the 2020 Galwan clash.
This operational tension persists despite a series of high-profile diplomatic engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping. Since October 2024, the two leaders have met three times-first in Kazan during the BRICS Summit, then in Tianjin in August 2025, and most recently in New Delhi in September 2026. While these meetings were framed as a strategic reset, with President Xi describing India as a "partner, not a rival," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal emphasized that peace and tranquility in border areas remain an essential prerequisite for the broader development of bilateral ties.
The gap between diplomatic optimism and border volatility has triggered a sharp political backlash. The Congress party has demanded a comprehensive statement from the Prime Minister in Parliament, arguing that the government is maintaining a "deafening silence" on the actual status of patrolling rights. Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge specifically highlighted reports of incursions near Taksing in August and questioned why confrontations continue even 47 days after Corps Commander-level talks at Wacha-Damai.
The central point of contention for the opposition is whether India's pre-May 2020 patrolling access has been fully restored. By contrasting the "hugplomacy" of summit photo opportunities with the ITBP's admission of ongoing face-offs, critics argue that a policy of diplomatic accommodation may be masking a failure to resolve structural territorial disputes in Arunachal Pradesh.
While the MEA continues to rely on existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to avoid "miscalculation," the internal restructuring of the ITBP indicates that India is preparing for a prolonged period of asymmetric friction, where diplomatic agreements and tactical border skirmishes coexist as parallel realities.

articles.title: The Cost of Separation: How U.S. Visa Rules and Trade Barriers Are Accelerating India’s Rise as a Global Innovation Hub - The Indian EYE
articles.summary: The Cost of Separation: How U.S. Visa Rules and Trade Barriers Are Accelerating India’s Rise as a Global Innovation Hub  The Indian EYE
articles.full_text:
Why restrictions on talent mobility and rising trade costs may strengthen India’s position in technology, pharmaceuticals, and global research.
By H. S. Panaser
The United States and India are entering a new phase of economic interdependence, shaped increasingly by immigration restrictions, trade barriers, technological competition and the global search for specialized talent. American policies designed to strengthen domestic employment, encourage manufacturing and reduce dependence on overseas operations are creating a complex set of consequences. While these measures may stimulate investment in selected US industries, they may also encourage multinational corporations to expand sophisticated research, engineering and technology operations in India.
This development presents an important paradox. Policies intended to bring jobs and innovation back to America may, in certain sectors, accelerate India’s emergence as a global innovation hub. The transformation is particularly visible in information technology, artificial intelligence, pharmaceuticals, clinical research and Global Capability Centers (GCCs).
India is no longer merely a destination for low-cost outsourcing. It is increasingly becoming a strategic location for product development, intellectual property creation, advanced analytics, drug research and multinational corporate decision-making. Understanding this shift is essential to evaluating the future of US–India economic relations.
The Changing Economics of Global Talent
American immigration policy has become an important factor in corporate workforce planning. Higher sponsorship costs, uncertainty surrounding skilled-worker visas, evolving H-1B selection rules and employment-based green-card processing constraints can complicate long-term decisions about hiring and retaining international professionals.
The policy objective of protecting American workers is legitimate. The United States must invest in domestic STEM education, technical training and opportunities for its graduates. However, specialized disciplines such as artificial intelligence, semiconductor engineering, medicinal chemistry, biotechnology and advanced software architecture require highly developed skills that cannot always be supplied immediately through domestic recruitment.
When qualified professionals cannot readily relocate to the United States, multinational corporations face several choices: increase domestic compensation, invest in training, delay projects or establish teams where suitable talent is available. Increasingly, India offers an attractive option because of its engineering workforce, established technology ecosystem and growing research infrastructure.
This creates a consequential economic reality: restricting the movement of talent does not necessarily bring the work home; sometimes the work moves to the talent. Instead of transferring engineers and scientists to American headquarters, companies may expand their operations in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and other Indian innovation centers.
Such decisions are not driven by immigration policy alone. They also reflect market access, corporate strategy, available skills and operating costs. Nevertheless, restrictive talent policies can reinforce the business case for developing advanced capabilities outside the United States.
Global Capability Centers: From Cost Savings to Innovation
India’s GCC industry illustrates this transformation. Originally established primarily to deliver support services and reduce operating expenses, many GCCs now perform functions that were previously concentrated near multinational headquarters.
These include AI development, cybersecurity, cloud architecture, advanced engineering, financial analytics, product design, clinical research support, regulatory documentation and enterprise technology strategy.
Industry estimates place India’s GCC sector in the tens of billions of dollars in annual economic activity, with continued expansion expected as more companies establish centers and existing facilities move into higher-value functions. Forecasts suggesting a market exceeding $100 billion should be understood as projections rather than realized revenue.
The significance of this expansion extends beyond employment. GCCs can deepen India’s participation in product design, proprietary research and intellectual property development. Ownership of resulting intellectual property may remain with the multinational parent, but the location of research activity, scientific expertise and technical leadership increasingly matters.
Alongside established GCCs, India is witnessing the development of specialized startups, engineering firms, contract research organizations and technology service providers that function as strategic partners to global corporations. These enterprises can deliver AI applications, software architecture, pharmaceutical analytics and engineering solutions without requiring every specialist to relocate overseas.
The result is an evolving economic model in which India is becoming not simply a provider of technical manpower, but an increasingly important contributor to global innovation.
Artificial Intelligence and the New Geography of Innovation
The growth of GCCs is especially significant for artificial intelligence. As AI becomes central to corporate competitiveness, companies need specialized professionals in machine learning, data engineering, cloud infrastructure, model development and cybersecurity. India’s combination of technical talent established enterprise relationships and expanding digital infrastructure makes it an important destination for these activities.
According to the 2026 Nasscom–Zinnov GCC Landscape Report, India hosted 2,117 GCCs, employing approximately 2.36 million professionals and generating $98.4 billion in annual revenue. The report also identifies AI as a major driver of the industry’s transformation from service delivery toward enterprise innovation.
These figures are important because they demonstrate that India’s innovation ecosystem is no longer an emerging possibility; it is already operating at considerable scale. American corporations can use Indian facilities for global product engineering and research while retaining strategic control of technology platforms and commercial markets. Meanwhile, Indian professionals gain experience in sophisticated technologies, strengthening the country’s capacity to develop its own intellectual property, startups and research enterprises.
Cost remains an advantage, although claims of uniform 60–70 percent savings require caution. Compensation varies substantially by skill, location and employer, while the total cost of a GCC includes infrastructure, management, security, regulatory compliance and coordination. Nevertheless, the combination of competitive operating costs and technical capability provides a strong commercial incentive for continued investment.
Pharmaceuticals: The Economics of Dependence and Resilience
The pharmaceutical sector presents an equally compelling example of US–India interdependence. According to the US Food and Drug Administration, nine out of ten prescriptions dispensed in America are for generic medicines, and approximately 40 percent of those generic products are manufactured in India. (Ref. OGPS)
This dependence has major implications for healthcare affordability and supply security. The Association for Accessible Medicines estimates that generic and biosimilar medicines collectively generated $496 billion in US healthcare savings during 2025. These savings reflect the entire generic and biosimilar market, not Indian manufacturers alone, but they demonstrate why preserving access to affordable medicines remains economically important. (Ref: Association for Accessible Medicines)
American policymakers have valid concerns about reliance on foreign pharmaceutical manufacturing, particularly for essential medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). However, moving pharmaceutical production is far more complicated than relocating an ordinary assembly operation. It requires substantial capital, validated processes, qualified scientific personnel, regulatory approvals and reliable supply chains.
Manufacturing costs in the United States are often higher than in India, particularly for labor-intensive, low-margin generic products. The precise difference depends on the product, technology and production scale. Consequently, wholesale relocation may not be commercially sustainable for every medicine.
A more practical solution is the dual-shore pharmaceutical model, under which Indian and American operations perform complementary functions. India can remain an important center for API production, complex generic synthesis, computational chemistry, clinical data analysis and regulatory documentation. American facilities can provide selected high-priority manufacturing, sterile production, final packaging, distribution, regulatory coordination and strategic inventory capacity.
This approach can improve supply-chain resilience while preserving the economics that make generic medicines affordable.
Major multinational pharmaceutical companies, including Eli Lilly, Bristol Myers Squibb, Pfizer and AstraZeneca, have developed substantial operations or research capabilities in India. Indian pharmaceutical companies such as Sun Pharma, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Zydus and Intas, through Accord Healthcare, have likewise built international commercial and manufacturing networks. These developments reflect a broader industry movement toward geographically distributed research, manufacturing and regulatory capabilities.
For Indian pharmaceutical companies, the next opportunity lies beyond traditional generics. Greater investment in complex formulations, biosimilars, novel drug delivery systems, biotechnology, clinical research and original drug discovery can help India move higher in the pharmaceutical value chain.

articles.title: US Midterm Polls: Democrats sniff opportunity, Trump fights to avoid a lame-duck presidency - The Times of India
articles.summary: US Midterm Polls: Democrats sniff opportunity, Trump fights to avoid a lame-duck presidency  The Times of IndiaVideo | US Midterm Elections | What You Need To Know About Trump's 2026 Midterm Elections  NDTVAs midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subject  The GuardianThe 3 Tests Before the Vote: What America’s Midterms Will Reveal  Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF)Can Democrats Sweep Congress From Trump? Michigan Lawmaker Rajeev Pu...
articles.full_text:
As Americans head into the final stretch of campaigning for the Nov 3 US midterm polls, both Democratic and Republican parties are set to field their big guns – and go on an ad-blitz – across key battleground states. Weighing on voters’ minds are issues like the rising cost of living, Trump’s war against Iran that has seen fuel prices skyrocket, healthcare and housing. Here’s a quick primer on what’s at stake in the polls, why it could be hugely consequential for the Trump presidency, and how it may shape US foreign policy.
Betting on the House: All 435 seats in Congress’s House of Representatives are up for grabs. Republicans hold a slim majority of 218 to Democrats’ 214 in the House. But this is widely expected to flip. That hinges on about 50 competitive races. Pollsters say Democrats could end up with a majority of as many as 15 seats.
Senatorial action: But it’s the Senate races that will determine whether Trump’s agenda over the next two years sinks or floats. The chamber has only 100 seats, but senators have staggered six-year terms. That means only 35 seats are up for grabs this time, of which about 10 are really competitive and likely to flip. 
If Democrats snag them up, they will overturn Republicans’ current majority of 53 to 45. Which is precisely why Republicans are pulling out all stops to boost their candidates in key races.
If Dems get House, GOP holds Senate:  A likely scenario, although Republicans have been shaken up by reported close contests in red states like Texas and Kansas. Plus, Trump’s approval rating is down – a record low for him at 31% in the latest poll. So, Republicans are divided over associating themselves with Trump’s policies. For some, getting the President’s endorsement may actually spell doom in tight races.
Midterm in numbers
But if Republicans do manage to hold onto their majority in Senate, Trump would still have room to manoeuvre and, more importantly, bat down political challenges emanating from a Democrats-dominated House.
If Dems win both houses: That’s the nightmare scenario Trump and GOP are trying to avoid. If Democrats control both the House and Senate, they effectively gain control of the legislative agenda. Sure, Democrats would still have to contend with Trump’s veto power – he could use that to block any Democrats-led legislation. And overturning a presidential veto requires two-thirds majority in both houses – a rarity.
But Democrats could still prove a point by forcing Trump to exercise his veto. That in turn could have political implications for presidential polls in 2028, putting Republicans looking for a post-Trump future in a tight spot. Also, unlike the House where a simple majority passes legislation, for bills to pass Senate they require a supermajority of 60 votes. Still, this is a scenario that GOP would like to avoid at all costs.
Key races: Naturally, most of them focus on Senate seats.
- In North Carolina, Democratic candidate Roy Cooper is leading in the polls over Republican candidate Michael Whatley. This is a seat GOP appears to be giving up on, holding back on ad spends in the final two weeks. 
- Texas is turning out to be a humdinger. Polls show a tight race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. Talarico is pegged to be slightly ahead at this point. And if he pulls it off on election day, Dems would end their 32-year losing streak in the state. But Republicans are pouring big money into this race, and are slated to outspend Democrats by three times, with overall GOP ad spend on this race set to cross $380mn. 
- Kansas, likewise, is witnessing a neck-to-neck race where Democrat Adam Hamilton is squaring off against GOP senator Roger Marshall. Recent polls showed there’s practically nothing to separate the two candidates. If Democrats win here, it would be historic – the state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in 94 years. 
- The race in Michigan is grabbing a lot of eyeballs, thanks to Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed who is going up against Republican Mike Rogers. Trump himself has taken potshots at El-Sayed, calling him a Muslim radical, while other Republican leaders have tried to associate him with the Muslim Brotherhood. If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim senator in US history. 
If Democrats win back both houses, it would certainly reduce space for Trump to act unilaterally on the foreign policy front. However, there are many ways in which Trump could work around any restrictions. For example, his war against Iran has skirted around the 60-day window for congressional approval through White House’s clever classification of the military action as aimed at ‘protecting American people’. Trump has also argued that since the war has started and stopped several times, the 60-day window for approval has renewed each time.
However, if Democrats control Congress, they could curtail any funding for that war. Conversely, they could also try to fast track funding support for Ukraine. But Trump could veto that or simply not act. So, it could be a stalemate between Trump and a Democrats-controlled Congress.
A third impeachment: A nuclear option, but not beyond the realm of possibility if Democrats win Congress. More likely though would be Democrats taking control of several committees, launching investigations against Trump officials or Trump family members, and blocking Trump’s appointments to key govt positions and roles, essentially leading to a lame-duck presidency.

articles.title: Exclusive-India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermining India-UK pact benefits, trade group says - Yahoo
articles.summary: Exclusive-India's Scotch probe of Diageo, Pernod undermining India-UK pact benefits, trade group says  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
By Aditya Kalra
NEW DELHI, Oct 23 (Reuters) - India's move to exclude bulk Scotch imports from a reduced 75% tariff goes against provisions agreed in an India-UK trade deal, a group representing liquor makers Diageo and Pernod Ricard wrote in a letter seen by Reuters.
Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of protracted negotiations leading up to the deal's July 15 implementation, though India ultimately agreed to halve import taxes on certain Scotch imports from 150% to 75% immediately and to 40% over 10 years.
The British government said "iconic UK products" like whiskies would benefit from the pact. Indian investigators, however, have privately told companies the reduced rate does not apply to bulk Scotch concentrates, creating the first significant dispute over the free trade agreement since it took effect.
India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence searched the offices of Pernod and Diageo and questioned executives this month as part of an investigation into whether they misclassified imported products to benefit from the reduced rate.
In a letter to the commerce minister on Friday, the International Spirits and Wines Association of India (ISWAI) wrote that the classification issue "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom."
"The preferential tariff treatment negotiated ... could effectively become unavailable for these imports," continued the letter, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.
ISWAI declined to comment on its letter, while India's commerce ministry did not immediately respond.
Pernod, which counts India as its biggest market by volume, declined to comment, and Diageo did not respond to a request for comment. Both told Reuters earlier this week that they were cooperating with Indian authorities carrying out the investigation.
BIG IMPLICATIONS FOR INDIA'S DRINKS SECTOR
Import tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, who have in the past faced demands for large amounts of back-tax. Such disputes have embroiled the likes of Samsung and Volkswagen.
Pernod is already facing antitrust cases in India and a $314 million back-tax demand from Indian authorities, who accuse it of undervaluing some imports. The company denies wrongdoing.
ISWAI's letter underscores the shockwaves the investigation has sent through India's $65 billion alcohol market. Britain accounts for almost 75% of India's imported spirits, primarily driven by Scotch whisky, according to Crisil Ratings.
Indian government inspectors have told companies that they do not benefit from the reduced 75% tariff on bulk imports of Scotch concentrates, which must be declared under a customs classification that attracts a 150% duty, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Pernod and Diageo import bulk concentrates, mixing them with other ingredients to produce hugely popular Indian brands like Royal Stag, Blenders Pride and McDowell's.
The three people said companies including Diageo and Pernod believe concentrates imported from Britain should benefit from the new, lower tariff. And ISWAI said in its letter that the India–UK agreement expressly provides preferential tariff treatment for whisky under the relevant tariff lines.
An urgent clarification could ensure market-access benefits negotiated by India and Britain are realised "while avoiding uncertainty and disruption for legitimate industry participants," the letter said.
(Reporting by Aditya Kalra; Additional reporting by Shivangi Acharya; Editing by Joe Bavier)

articles.title: US Secretary of State's visit to India: New opportunities, old obstacles. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: US Secretary of State's visit to India: New opportunities, old obstacles.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's two-day visit to India this week sends positive signals about the prospects for bilateral relations after a period of tension.
However, according to Professor Harsh V. Pant, Vice President of the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) of India , the gap between political pronouncements and actual outcomes remains significant, as both countries must balance economic interests, strategic calculations, and geopolitical shifts.
Trade has not seen a breakthrough.
Speaking to a Vietnam News Agency (VNA) reporter in New Delhi, Professor Harsh V. Pant assessed Foreign Minister Rubio's statement that the US and India were "very close" to a bilateral trade agreement as a positive sign. However, he believed there was not enough basis to confirm that the two sides would finalize an agreement in the next few weeks as the US had hoped.
US-India trade negotiations have dragged on for over a year and have repeatedly encountered obstacles. The recent admission by the Indian Finance Minister that the negotiations are stalled suggests that there is little room left for concessions between the two sides. Mr. Pant stated: “The most significant obstacle now lies in market access, particularly the degree of openness India can offer to US businesses in the agricultural sector. This has long been a ‘red line’ for New Delhi in trade negotiations.”
In addition, India needs to ensure favorable access to the US market for its domestic goods, especially those with a competitive advantage. Other issues such as the H-1B visa, conditions for the movement of Indian labor in the context of the Trump administration's tough immigration policies, and the final tariffs Washington will impose on Indian goods will also affect New Delhi's calculations.
Therefore, the ORF Vice President believes that trade negotiations may make progress in the near future, but it is not yet possible to determine a conclusion. He expects the two countries to make concrete progress by the end of the year, given that India is also pushing for trade agreements with other partners, including Canada.
Energy leverage
While the outlook for trade remains uncertain, energy is emerging as a sector that could provide further impetus to US-India relations. However, the potential for cooperation still depends on both sides reconciling their differences in interests and policies.
Professor Pant noted that the trip by US officials to Mumbai, India's financial center, and Jamnagar, a major oil refining hub, took place against the backdrop of significant adjustments in Washington's approach to energy. These moves, including the postponement of tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and information regarding oil transactions, suggest that US policy needs to be viewed in relation to its own energy needs.
You may also like
Mr. Pant stated: “The core issue is that when faced with essential economic needs, no country is willing to easily give up its interests. That is why I believe energy can absolutely develop into a mutually beneficial area of cooperation between India and the US, instead of continuing to be a source of disagreement.”
With a population of around 1.5 billion and over 85% of its crude oil needs dependent on imports, India is particularly sensitive to price fluctuations, supply disruptions, and shifts in the strategies of major oil-producing countries. New Delhi's increased purchases of Russian oil at discounted prices following the outbreak of conflict in Ukraine , despite disagreements with Washington, reflects its priority of ensuring energy security and maintaining strategic autonomy.
According to Pant, India is unlikely to abandon its Russian oil supply simply because of US pressure. Instead, Washington appears to be seeking to expand cooperation by proposing that Indian refineries participate in processing Venezuelan heavy oil, serving both the US and international markets.
With its large refining capacity, India can meet domestic demand while also participating more deeply in the international energy supply chain. Professor Pant believes this shows that the US is viewing New Delhi not only as a trade partner but also as a crucial partner in the energy sector.
For New Delhi, energy cooperation with Washington only makes sense if it creates concrete benefits for energy security, supplements supply sources, and diversifies options, rather than restricting existing partner networks or undermining India's autonomy.
Strategic barriers
Professor Pant stated that the prospects for US-India cooperation are also affected by two factors. Firstly, Indian public opinion is increasingly skeptical about the reliability of the US under President Trump. Therefore, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government needs to demonstrate that agreements with Washington bring tangible benefits to the economy and the people.
Secondly, India is expanding its economic relations with a wider range of partners, rather than relying on a single market. Trade negotiations with Canada and other partners provide New Delhi with more options, allowing it to maintain a proactive position in negotiations with the US.
The inconsistency in Washington's energy approach also raises questions about the sustainability of cooperation. On the one hand, the US pressures India to reduce its purchases of Russian oil; on the other hand, Washington takes actions related to oil transactions with Moscow. Rubio's admission that India cannot immediately find alternative sources of Russian oil suggests that the US administration recognizes, to some extent, the practical limitations that New Delhi faces.
You may also like
In this context, the proposed cooperation in processing Venezuelan oil could help the US expand its influence in the energy supply chain, while also providing India with more options. However, the practical effectiveness of this approach remains to be seen.
More broadly, Foreign Minister Rubio's visit demonstrates that energy is increasingly intertwined with geopolitical calculations, not simply a commercial issue. While disagreements over tariffs and Russian oil remain unresolved, energy cooperation could become a new pillar of US-India relations, but it also risks further fueling friction if the parties link this sector too closely to political concessions.
According to Professor Pant's analysis, the two countries need to maintain stable relations and gradually expand cooperation based on genuine mutual benefit. Linking energy deals too closely to trade concessions could limit India's flexibility. A sustainable agreement needs to incentivize diversified trade and investment while respecting each side's strategic autonomy.
The prospects for US-India relations will therefore depend not only on political goodwill but also on the ability to translate declarations into concrete results, harmonize interests, and address existing differences.

articles.title: ‘Enough clean chits to China’: Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress questions PM Modi over security, trade | India News - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: ‘Enough clean chits to China’: Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress questions PM Modi over security, trade | India News  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
Kharge’s remarks came after ITBP chief Shatrujeet Kapoor said that face-offs with Chinese PLA troops were continuing along the Arunachal Pradesh border
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Friday questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi over India’s national and economic security in relation to China, citing reported ongoing face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh and the widening trade deficit between the two countries.
“Enough clean chits to China. PM Modi must come clean before India!” Kharge said in a post on X, accusing the government of “keeping the nation in the dark” over border security.
Kharge’s remarks came after Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) director general Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor said on Friday that face-offs with Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops were continuing at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border. The developments follow reports of face-offs in the Taksing area and Corps Commander-level talks held at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point to address tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
In his post, Kharge referred to reports of Chinese incursions near Taksing in August and questioned whether India’s patrolling access had been compromised. He also asked whether the confrontations signalled the possibility of another serious border crisis after the Galwan clash in June 2020, in which 20 Indian Army personnel were killed.
“Has India’s patrolling access been compromised? Arunachal Pradesh is an inseparable part of India. Why is the nation being kept in the dark?” Kharge questioned.
Since July, there have been reports of a standoff with Chinese troops in the remote Taksin area of Upper Subansiri district. Asked about this in a press conference in August, foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the state of border affairs has ramifications for overall India-China ties, adding that the two sides have agreed to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to “avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation” along the border.
Kharge's concern
Raising concerns over India’s trade relationship with China, Kharge said, “Chinese imports have surged 102 per cent, while India's trade deficit with China has ballooned 155 per cent to $112.16 billion. Even Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman admits China obstructs Indian exports.”
He questioned the government’s reported moves to ease investment restrictions and consider production-linked incentive (PLI) benefits for eligible China-linked ventures. “Has Make in India become Import from China?” he asked.
Kharge also questioned the outcomes of India’s diplomatic engagements with Beijing, saying, “What tangible results have these engagements delivered? Have India’s pre-May 2020 patrolling rights been fully restored?”
The government has in the past rejected the Congress's allegations of bowing down to Beijing, saying it was committed to protecting India's borders.
At the same time, BJP functionaries have accused the Congress of politicising national security issues. They have also hit back at the opposition party, saying Jawaharlal Nehru ceded ground to China.
India and China have attempted to rebuild their relationship after reaching an understanding in October 2024 to end a military standoff in Ladakh that lasted more than four years and took ties to a six-decade low. Chinese President Xi Jinping made his first visit to India in seven years to attend the BRICS Summit on September 12-13, and held a bilateral meeting with PM Modi to review ties.
Speaking at an Asia Society event in New York in late September, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said India-China ties were better today than they were a couple of years ago.
Congress criticism
Congress criticised PM Modi for meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit while face-offs were reportedly ongoing along the Arunachal Pradesh border. Kharge, meanwhile, said national security demanded accountability rather than what he termed “diplomatic photo opportunities” and “Hugplomacy”.
“Imagine—one side, China was clashing with our soldiers; on the other, Modi was welcoming China’s president. It’s like rubbing salt in the wounds of our soldiers,” the party said on their official X handle.
“Sometimes giving China a clean chit, sometimes abandoning control of patrolling points and the country's land. This weak Prime Minister has caused immense damage to the country,” the party added.

articles.title: Resign Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, says Trump over Ilhan Omar's birth name dispute - India Today
articles.summary: Resign Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, says Trump over Ilhan Omar's birth name dispute  India TodayWhy is Trump questioning Ilhan Omar’s name?  Al JazeeraRep. Ilhan Omar details early-morning raid she says was ‘designed’ to ‘freak’ her out  MS NOW‘Openly admitted to fraud’: Trump demands Ilhan Omar’s resignation from Congress over ‘fake name’ claim  The Times of IndiaWhat Ilhan Omar’s “Not To My Knowledge” Teaches Us About Leadership Communication  Forbes
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has demanded Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's resignation, claiming she used a fake name to enter Congress. Trump's demand follows a court filing that listed her as 'Ilhan Nur Said Elmi' and comes days after federal agents raided her Washington home, seizing her passport and phone, and reportedly collecting her DNA samples.
"Ilhan Nur Said Elmi" is the name US President Donald Trump wants Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to answer for, demanding her resignation over what he calls a case of fraud.
Trump on Friday called on Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to resign, alleging that she used a false name to enter Congress after a Justice Department court filing identified her as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar". Trump also invoked longstanding, unproven allegations that Omar married her brother, as a federal investigation into her immigration history continues.
In a post on Truth Social on Friday (October 23), Trump said Omar had used a "fake name" to be sworn into Congress and claimed she had "openly admitted to fraud". The US President urged House Speaker James Michael Johnson to be informed that Omar should immediately resign, arguing that she could no longer legally serve as a member of Congress.
Trump's post followed an October 21 court filing in which federal prosecutors used the name "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi" before listing "Ilhan Abdullahi Omar" as an alternative name. The filing, connected to requests to unseal records relating to the search of Omar's Washington home, did not explain the naming convention or establish that she had committed fraud. The abbreviation "a/k/a" means "also known as" and does not, by itself, prove that a person used a false identity.
Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who was born in Somalia and became a naturalised US citizen in 2000, has rejected allegations of immigration fraud. No public finding has established that she fraudulently obtained citizenship or used a false name to enter Congress.
On October 12, federal agents raided Ilhan Omar's Washington home, seizing 17 items, including phones and documents. Some reports said that investigators obtained her DNA sample. Omar denied that a sample was collected during the search. The Minnesota Congresswoman has since said she will move out over safety concerns.
WHY TRUMP IS QUESTIONING ILHAN OMAR'S NAME
The name controversy centres on the surname Elmi, which Omar shares with her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. The two married legally in Minnesota in February 2009. Omar has said their relationship ended in 2011 and that they divorced under Islamic tradition that year, although their legal divorce was finalised in 2017.
Omar subsequently legally married Ahmed Abdisalan Hirsi in January 2018, according to public records. The couple had three children together. Ilhan Omar filed for divorce from Ahmed Hirsi, the father of her three children, in October 2019, citing an "irretrievable breakdown" of their marriage, and the divorce was finalised the following month.
The allegation that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was Omar's biological brother has circulated among conservative commentators since at least 2016. Critics have alleged that she married him to help him obtain US immigration status. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, calling it false and offensive.
The latest controversy intensified after Omar was asked about the allegation in an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes on October 21. Hayes asked whether there was any "weird kernel of truth" to the claim that she was related to her former husband. Omar replied, "Not to my knowledge."
Omar said the allegation originated with a Somali blog and was subsequently amplified by right-wing commentators. Her answer has since been cited by critics questioning her account, but it is not an admission that she married her brother.
Meanwhile, Collin Rugg, co-owner of Trending Politics, a right-wing news and commentary platform, also highlighted the potential legal implications of the name dispute, citing former Minnesota federal immigration judge Nathan Hansen. Hansen told Fox News that if Omar had lived under an alias, government forms she had filled out over the years could come under scrutiny, potentially raising questions about sworn documents and even wire fraud.
Notably, the search of Omar's home took place a fortnight before the November midterm elections, in which she is seeking re-election in Minnesota. It must also be noted that Trump's approval ratings have been at a record low due to the Iran war and inflation in the US.
ILHAN OMAR'S DNA SAMPLE OBTAINED IN FEDERAL PROBE
The name dispute comes amid a federal investigation into Omar's immigration history. Federal agents searched her Washington, DC, residence on October 12 under a judicially authorised warrant. Reports said investigators seized her cellphone and passport, while the investigation has also involved subpoenas issued to some of her relatives.
Fox News reported that investigators had obtained a DNA sample from Omar. The Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security have not publicly explained how the sample was collected or what it is intended to establish. Reports have differed on the circumstances surrounding the collection of genetic material.
The investigation is reportedly examining allegations concerning Omar's immigration paperwork, including questions about her date of birth and information submitted by her late father. Authorities have not publicly disclosed evidence establishing that she committed immigration fraud, and the purpose of the reported DNA evidence remains unclear.
The controversy over her former marriage is separate from the questions about her immigration and naturalisation records. Reports suggest that even if investigators examine possible family relationships through DNA evidence, the existence of a sample alone does not establish that Omar and Elmi are siblings or that their marriage involved immigration fraud.
Omar has described the search of her home as politically motivated. Her lawyers have challenged the federal action and demanded the return of seized property. The Trump administration has maintained that the investigation is a law-enforcement matter.
Trump's latest demand for Omar's resignation adds a political dimension to the investigation less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, in which she is seeking re-election to represent Minnesota's 5th Congressional District.
