articles.title: India’s Dhampur Bio Organics Signs Exclusive Mycoprotein Production Deal with Planetary - Green Queen Media
articles.summary: India’s Dhampur Bio Organics Signs Exclusive Mycoprotein Production Deal with Planetary  Green Queen Media
articles.full_text:
Indian sugar giant Dhampur Bio Organics has partnered with Swiss fermentation startup Planetary to produce mycoprotein products through the latter’s BioBlocks platform.
Months after they began exploring a tech licensing partnership to bring mycoprotein production to India, Dhampur Bio Organics (DBO) and Planetary have signed a 10-year deal to manufacture sustainable protein and fibre ingredients.
DBO will turn sugar and molasses into high-value microbial ingredients on an industrial scale through Planetary’s full-scale biomass and precision fermentation platform, titled BioBlocks.
Planetary will act as the tech provider and offtaker of the products, while DBO will be focused on constructing and operating mycoprotein production infrastructure. The two companies plan to establish a joint venture dedicated to executing additional commercialisation and offtake agreements.
“This step means nutritional access where 73% of the population is protein-deficient, supply resilience where 98% of whey and plant proteins are imported, 30% cost reduction when exporting the product into the Western markets, [and] gradually branching into the production of adjacent bioeconomy foods and products,” Planetary co-founder and CEO David Brandes said in a LinkedIn post.
Planetary and Dhampur Bio Organics fuel India’s biomanufacturing boom
Planetary operates a full-scale fermentation platform encompassing bioprocess design, scale-up, and industrial manufacturing, which is built to support the development and industrialisation of future-facing food and material solutions using a wide array of feedstocks.
The company’s initial focus is on biomass-fermented mycoprotein, but the bioprocess competency of its Bioblocks platform has also enabled it to help blue-chip CPG and startups bring precision-fermented products to life, including proteins, fats, colouring agents, enzymes, and biomaterials.
The company is expanding this sugar-to-protein upcycling tech globally, including plans to enable ultra-low-cost mycoprotein production (under $1 per kg) via partnerships with industrial players in sucrose-rich and protein-deficient geographies.
Tech licensing to agro-industrial partners (particularly sugar companies) is at the heart of its IP-rich strategy, enabling the conversion of low-value byproducts into high-value proteins, fibre and enzymes. This, the company says, unlocks a “new circular bioeconomy”.
Some of these partners include Swiss firm Schweizer Zucker, Dutch cooperative Royal Cosun, and DBO. Planetary has been in talks with the latter since January, as part of a biomanufacturing boom in India.
In 2024, Bengaluru saw the launch of the Centre for Smart Protein and Sustainable Material Innovation (an incubation hub) and the Alternative Proteins Innovation Center (a scale-up facility). And last year, the government opened an animal stem cell biobank, in Hyderabad, followed by the launch of an incubation centre for R&D on technologies like precision fermentation and CRISPR this March.
And this week alone, Israeli startup Brevel teamed up with The Wave Group to build a joint venture factory in Uttar Pradesh that uses illuminated fermentation to create microalgae-based ingredients.
Sugar partnership and licensing model ‘no longer a concept’
As part of the licensing agreement, DBO will pay Planetary a royalty worth 10% of after-tax revenue each quarter. The latter will also receive a one-time fee covering engineering, project launch, installation, commissioning, process training and handover support, and an IT setup fee for the configuration of the Swiss firm’s data platform.
According to a filing on the Bombay Stock Exchange, Planetary’s key obligations in the partnership will be to provide licensed IP and technical services, support launch, installation and training, maintain and enforce the licensed IP, and offer ongoing technical assistance.
Meanwhile, DBO’s role includes the payment of fees and royalties, compliance with confidentiality and audits, protection of the IP licence, and obtaining the required regulatory approvals.
“The technology to be used for production of mycoprotein products has synergy with the existing business of the company and forward integration step, wherein sugar and molasses will act as feedstock for production of mycoprotein,” DBO noted in its filing.
Planetary, which raised $28M earlier this year to expand its technology and product portfolio, suggested that its collaborations prove that its “sugar partnership and licensing model is no longer a concept; it’s a global footprint”. “We’re turning sugar mills into […] ingredient producers and protein factories, that’s the circular bioeconomy,” it said in a LinkedIn post.
The DBO partnership aligns with India’s BioE3 strategy, which focuses on accelerating tech development and commercialisation by setting up biomanufacturing hubs and biofoundries across the country.
The government has also published a roadmap to boost the national bioeconomy sector, with a target value of $2.6T by 2047. Within this, it plans to more than triple the value of the biotech sector, from $195B today to $691B in 2035, underlining bioindustrials – which include alternative proteins, enzymes, and food-grade media – as the segment with the largest potential.

articles.title: China’s Two-Front Strategy Against India? Brahma Chellaney Flags Border and Economic Pressure - theopenpress.in
articles.summary: China’s Two-Front Strategy Against India? Brahma Chellaney Flags Border and Economic Pressure  theopenpress.in
articles.full_text:
Strategic affairs expert Brahma Chellaney has raised concerns about what he describes as China’s two-pronged approach towards India, involving pressure along the border and the use of economic restrictions. His comments come amid reports of continuing face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at several locations along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh.
According to Chellaney, Beijing could be seeking to constrain India’s progress through two channels: maintaining pressure along disputed border areas and using its position in global supply chains to influence access to important industrial equipment, battery technologies and critical minerals.
His assessment links recent border developments with China’s export policies. However, the interpretation of Beijing’s broader strategic intentions remains Chellaney’s analysis and should not be treated as an officially declared Chinese policy.
Read More: Read the full report on continuing India-China face-offs along the Arunachal Pradesh border
Why Is the Border Situation Drawing Attention?
Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Singh Kapur recently confirmed that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops were continuing at several locations near the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh.
Reacting to the development, Chellaney argued that China could be using territorial pressure and economic restrictions as complementary ways to affect India’s strategic and economic ambitions.
In his assessment, developments in Arunachal Pradesh deserve attention alongside the long-running border dispute in eastern Ladakh. He has argued that Chinese activity in these areas could be intended to influence the situation on the ground.
India and China have different perceptions of the LAC in several sectors. These differences have repeatedly complicated patrol activities and border management, leading to face-offs and diplomatic engagement between the two countries.
Tensions Around the Taksing Area
Media reports said Indian and Chinese patrol teams came face to face near the Taksing area in Arunachal Pradesh’s Upper Subansiri district in July 2026. Reports also referred to subsequent developments in other areas along the frontier.
The ITBP chief’s remarks indicate that some border-management challenges remain in Arunachal Pradesh. However, complete details of troop positions and the current situation at every location have not been made public.
The India-China boundary stretches for approximately 3,488 kilometres. In several sectors, the two sides have differing perceptions of the alignment of the LAC. Military and diplomatic mechanisms continue to play a role in managing these differences and preventing local incidents from escalating.
Read More: Read about India-China border talks and the agreed mechanisms for managing the LAC
The Economic Pressure Argument
Chellaney has also pointed to Chinese export restrictions affecting certain industrial goods and materials. These include manufacturing equipment, industrial components, battery technologies and critical minerals, according to his assessment.
Such materials are important for sectors including electronics, battery manufacturing, energy storage and advanced industrial production. When a country relies heavily on a limited number of suppliers, restrictions or disruptions can affect production schedules, costs and plans to expand manufacturing capacity.
Chellaney argues that China’s position in global supply chains gives it the ability to exert economic influence. In his view, India’s ambition to become a larger global manufacturing hub makes reliable access to industrial inputs and alternative suppliers increasingly important.
The intention behind individual export restrictions, however, must be assessed on the basis of the relevant rules, official announcements and their demonstrated effects. The existence of a restriction alone does not establish its full strategic purpose.
Why Supply-Chain Security Matters to India
India has been seeking to expand manufacturing in areas such as electronics, batteries, clean energy and semiconductors. These industries require reliable supplies of specialised machinery, components and minerals.
Dependence on a single country or a narrow group of suppliers can create vulnerabilities when trade restrictions, geopolitical disputes or supply disruptions occur. Diversifying supply chains and developing domestic manufacturing capabilities can therefore help reduce exposure to external shocks.
The challenge for India is to continue benefiting from international trade while reducing dependence in sectors that are particularly important for industrial development and national security.

The India-China relationship involves more than the territorial dispute. Trade, technology and economic interdependence are also important parts of the relationship.
The two countries have maintained military and diplomatic channels, including commander-level meetings and discussions between special representatives. These mechanisms are intended to maintain peace along the border, reduce misunderstandings and manage disputes through dialogue.

A balanced assessment requires more than one expert’s interpretation. Official information, trade data, export-control measures and verified developments along the border are all relevant to understanding the wider situation.

Three areas are likely to remain important for India: maintaining border preparedness, diversifying supplies of critical industrial materials and continuing diplomatic engagement with China.
Vigilance along the frontier remains important for security. Meanwhile, diversified supply chains and stronger domestic manufacturing capabilities can reduce the impact of external disruptions. The US Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola while another candidate with the same name remains on the ballot.
The case could trigger a wider legal battle between the Trump administration and state authorities over the certification of election results, particularly in races where Republicans face a risk of losing seats.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Alaska on Thursday, argues that the state must protect the integrity of federal elections. It asks the court to block the certification of a Peltola victory if Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate from the small fishing community of Petersburg, remains on the ballot.
“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says.
Republicans have alleged that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to draw votes away from the incumbent senator. However, he has said he entered the race independently.
Two candidates with the same name on ballot
The Alaska Senate race has attracted attention because its outcome could help determine which party controls the Senate. 
Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Peltola, a former congresswoman.
Daniel J. Sullivan will also appear on the ballot without a party designation, while the senator will be identified as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference, meaning voters confused by the two names could select both.
The Alaska Supreme Court has already rejected an earlier Republican attempt to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot. Republican officials in the state also made the decisions about how the two candidates would be listed.
Neither the senator's campaign nor Daniel J. Sullivan immediately responded to requests for comment.
The Trump administration has increasingly used the Justice Department to pursue legal action against political opponents and Democratic-controlled states ahead of elections. Democrats and voting rights advocates have warned that the administration could try to prevent the certification of results in races lost by Trump's party, drawing comparisons with the president's unsuccessful attempts to overturn his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department did not intend to interfere improperly in elections.
“It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters in Virginia on Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed.
The lawsuit was signed by Associate US Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and defendants in cases related to the January 6 attack on the US Capitol before joining the department's senior leadership.
Legal challenge faces questions over its merits
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the case would probably become relevant only if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race. He also questioned whether the lawsuit had a sound legal basis.
“The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” he said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The US Constitution gives states the authority to administer their elections, while federal elections must also follow standards set by Congress. Trump has repeatedly sought to change election procedures through executive orders, several of which have been blocked by courts.
Certifying an election is the formal process through which a state confirms the winner. The Justice Department's lawsuit seeks to stop that process in a specific set of circumstances in Alaska.
The state's ranked choice voting system could further complicate the race. The system allows voters to rank candidates by preference, with votes redistributed as candidates are eliminated until a winner emerges. Trump opposes the system, and a separate ballot measure will ask voters whether it should be repealed. The final result could take weeks to determine.
Trump calls rival candidate's presence ‘cheating’
Trump has repeatedly criticised Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, raising the issue at a rally in Alaska this month and in social media posts.
In a post on Wednesday, he wrote, “We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,”
In another post this week, Trump described the situation as “CHEATING.”
Candidates with similar names have long been used in US elections in attempts to divert votes from a rival. Such tactics can be particularly significant in closely contested races.
Republicans have also been linked to an effort to encourage Ohio voters to support a socialist candidate in that state's Senate race. The move could help Republican Senator Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

US President Donald Trump has revived his threat of intervention in Cuba, suggesting that American warships returning from the war with Iran could stop near the island before secretary of state Marco Rubio steps in to negotiate a deal.
Speaking at a rally in South Florida on Friday, Trump responded to a question shouted by someone in the crowd about Cuba. His remarks came just days before the US midterm elections, with voters concerned about rising prices of essentials, including fuel and groceries, amid the war with Iran.
“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”
Trump had floated a similar idea earlier this year but had not raised it publicly in recent months. He has repeatedly suggested that Cuba could become the next focus of US intervention after the Iran war, which he has long predicted would wind down but has not yet ended.
Trump and Rubio turn up pressure on Cuba
Trump and Rubio have both adopted a hard line towards Cuba's communist government. In May, the two renewed the possibility of US military intervention, with the threat gaining further significance after the Trump administration announced criminal charges against former Cuban leader Raúl Castro.
Trump told reporters in the Oval Office at the time that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades, adding that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it.”
Rubio has argued that Cuba poses a national security threat because of its relationships with countries hostile to the US. Although he has said Washington wants to resolve its differences with Havana peacefully, he has expressed doubts about reaching a diplomatic agreement with the island's current leadership.
Shortly after Trump's speech on Friday, Rubio posted on social media that “now is the time” for action on Cuba. Addressing those seeking to bring about change on the island, he urged them “to seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.”
Rubio has not spoken extensively about Cuba in recent weeks. In a September 29 interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, he described the island's economic and political situation in stark terms.
“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without referring to any CIA operation.
“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing,” he said. “We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”
Talks continue as Washington tightens sanctions
Despite the increasingly tough rhetoric, US and Cuban officials have held meetings in recent months to explore ways to improve relations. Trump administration officials, including Rubio, have taken part in discussions with Cuban representatives.
However, the US side has emerged dissatisfied with the talks, leading Washington to impose further sanctions on the Cuban government.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump said Rubio was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”. He added that he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep.”
A few days later, Trump said he expected the two countries “will make a deal”, adding, “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”
The two countries also clashed at the United Nations earlier this week after the Trump administration sought to rally opposition to an annual resolution condemning Washington's decades-old economic embargo against Havana.
Cuba faces a deepening economic crisis
Cuba has been struggling with a severe economic and energy crisis since 2020. Its economy has contracted, while its population of around 10 million has faced widespread power cuts, food shortages and rising prices.
The crisis has also triggered repeated waves of public protests and a significant exodus of Cubans, with hundreds of thousands leaving the country, many heading to the United States.

Former Indian Army Chief General Manoj Mukund Naravane has said that the 2020 Galwan Valley clash demonstrated that China could not resolve its boundary dispute with India through military force. He emphasised that the long-standing dispute must be addressed through dialogue and diplomatic engagement.
Speaking at a gathering of information technology and banking professionals in Pune, Naravane said India had stood its ground during the confrontation and made it clear that unilateral attempts to alter the boundary through force would not be accepted.
His remarks have renewed attention on the consequences of the Galwan clash, India-China relations and ongoing efforts to manage the unresolved boundary dispute.
What Changed After the Galwan Clash?
In June 2020, Indian and Chinese troops were involved in a violent confrontation in the Galwan Valley in eastern Ladakh. Twenty Indian soldiers died in the incident, which severely affected bilateral relations and led to increased military deployments along the disputed frontier.
According to Naravane, India demonstrated after Galwan that it would not accept unilateral attempts to change the boundary. He said the developments had strengthened India's standing internationally in military, diplomatic and terms.
However, the boundary dispute remains unresolved. India and China continue to differ over the alignment and interpretation of the Line of Actual Control in several areas.
What Is the Difference Between a Border and a Boundary?
Naravane explained the distinction between the terms “border” and “boundary” during his address. He said a recognised international border is generally clearly defined and accepted by the countries concerned. By contrast, the India-China boundary remains disputed because the two sides do not agree on its entire alignment.
The India-China boundary stretches for approximately 3,488 kilometres. In several sectors, the two countries have differing perceptions of where the line runs. Patrols in these areas can therefore lead to face-offs and heightened tensions.
This is why a lasting resolution requires mutual understanding and an agreed settlement, rather than relying on military deployments alone.
Why Dialogue Remains Important
Naravane said resolving disputes through dialogue should remain India's first priority. He also made clear that a preference for negotiations does not mean compromising national security. In his view, the use of force should not be the first option, although it may remain an option of last resort depending on circumstances.
India and China have a Special Representatives mechanism to discuss the boundary question. India's National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi serve as the respective representatives.
At the 25th round of Special Representatives' talks in August 2026, both sides agreed to advance discussions on boundary delimitation and border management. They also reiterated the importance of using existing communication channels to prevent misunderstandings and tensions along the Line of Actual Control.

Naravane Also Refers to Operation Sindoor
During his address, Naravane also referred to Operation Sindoor. He said India had conveyed that it would not tolerate actions against it indefinitely and could respond where necessary.
He said India decided to stop the operation because, in its assessment, the intended objectives had been achieved. He also highlighted the importance of determining when to end a military operation, not just when to begin one.
His comments underlined the role of clearly defined objectives, operational control and timely decision-making in military action.
What Lies Ahead for India-China Relations?
The boundary dispute remains one of the major challenges in India-China relations. Both countries have pursued military and diplomatic engagement to reduce tensions, but a final settlement remains pending.
A key question is whether the two sides can translate practical progress in border management into a broader agreement on the boundary. Dialogue, military communication mechanisms and discussions on delimitation will remain important elements of that process.
Naravane's remarks are significant in this context. His message is that maintaining firmness on security does not rule out negotiations; rather, a durable resolution requires both preparedness and diplomacy.

The latest comments come amid continued efforts to stabilise relations following previous military tensions along the frontier. Any sustained confrontation could complicate those efforts, making transparency and communication between the two sides particularly important.
The next developments to watch are any clarification from the Defence Ministry on the reported face-offs, further military or diplomatic discussions, and whether both countries make progress on improving their understanding of disputed sections of the LAC. Essay
				  			
  					
  			 
			The Future Trajectory of Bangladesh’s Foreign Policy					
						
		
		
Views from Emerging Leaders					
						
				 
		
Md. Tanvir Habib examines the renewed national debate within Bangladesh about its role in the world, drawing on original research he conducted with the emerging leaders of the country’s major political parties.
Since the violent ouster of the autocratic regime of Sheikh Hasina in July–August 2024, Bangladesh has undergone significant transformation. A key metric is changes to its foreign policy posture, which has shifted away from the long-standing India-favorable approach of the Sheikh Hasina regime[1] to one that is based on national interest, dignity, and strategic diversity.[2] Given the power disparity between both countries and India’s regional ambitions, the “India factor” has been an enduring issue in Bangladesh’s foreign policy.[3] Personal levels of trust and relations between Sheikh Hasina’s family and India’s Nehru-Gandhi family, ideological similarity between the Awami League and Indian National Congress party, and Hasina’s requirement for a regional patron shaped her party’s approach to India.[4] Likewise, India viewed all governments in Bangladesh not affiliated with the Awami League with distrust and suspicion. Bangladeshis came to view Hasina’s rule as an extension of India’s “big brotherly” attitude toward their country, with many accusing India of shielding Hasina’s fifteen-year-long authoritarian rule from international criticism.[5] Hasina’s evacuation from Bangladesh in 2024 led to the rapid deterioration of bilateral relations amid a broader reconsideration of Bangladesh’s foreign policy.
This essay examines the renewed national debate within Bangladesh about its role in the world. Given the prominence of students during the July uprising of 2024, youth views on foreign policy may be especially consequential for the future trajectory of Bangladesh’s external relations. Additionally, in the run up to the February 2026 elections, political parties contesting the national elections published their own foreign policy aspirations. This essay examines these documents. It also features original research from interviews I conducted with emerging leaders in Bangladesh’s three major political parties: the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), the student-led National Citizen Party (NCP), and the Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami (BJI).
Bangladesh Nationalist Party
The BNP’s historical shaping of Bangladesh’s foreign policy doctrine continues to influence decision-making with external partners. The party’s foreign policy outlook evolved under its founder, Ziaur Rahman. His idea of “Bangladeshi nationalism” based on territorial sovereignty, statehood, Muslim identity, and independent decision-making at the international level has had an outsized and lasting impact on Bangladesh’s foreign policy.[6] This was a clear departure from the then dominant “Bengali nationalism” championed by the ousted Awami League. While Bengali nationalism has its roots in the social and political initiatives before independence from Pakistan in 1971 to preserve Bengali ethnicity, language, and culture, Bangladeshi nationalism is based on the idea of “citizenship nationalism,” transcending the boundaries or parochiality of ethnic nationalism to a nationalism that is based on citizenship.
However, Bangladeshi nationalism is somewhat conditioned by majority culture and faith. This view has remained a constant theme and has emerged as the core of the “Bangladesh-centric approach” proposed by both the NCP and BJI, despite its origins in BNP doctrine. President Zia’s signature successes, including helping establish the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), signing the Ganges water-sharing agreement with India, and playing a lead role in Islamic affairs internationally, all helped shape a paradigm in foreign policy that no subsequent government has been able to overlook.[7] Perhaps owing to this independent way of thinking, the BNP’s worldview often prioritizes balanced relations in the region and globally to offset the influence of larger countries.[8] This was outlined in the BNP’s 2030 vision document, which stated that “Bangladesh has friends and no masters.”[9] Further exemplifying this philosophy were the party’s election slogans: “Bangladesh First” and “Friends Yes, Masters No.”[10] These were direct attacks targeted at both the ousted Awami League and BJI, which are accused by the BNP of maintaining subservient relations with India and Pakistan, respectively.
In terms of the party’s regional outlook, observers have tended to view the BNP as more skeptical of India than the Awami League. This skepticism is reflected in the agenda it outlines for the bilateral relationship. Recently, the BNP has emphasized a foreign policy approach based on equality, mutual respect, reciprocity, and resolution of outstanding bilateral issues, like the Teesta water-sharing dispute, trade imbalances, and border management.[11]
It was also during President Zia’s tenure that Bangladesh-China relations solidified. The BNP has historically maintained a favorable outlook toward China, but recently the party has increased its engagement with Beijing to remedy economic mismanagement that occurred under the Awami League–led government.[12] The BNP-led government requires massive investments to restore Bangladesh’s economic growth and reduce youth unemployment, and it has identified China as a major development partner toward that end. Cementing this approach has been the continuous visits of the party’s senior leadership and youth wing to China. At the same time, the BNP has maintained active engagement with Western countries for years, and on issues such as democratic legitimacy, the rule of law, and government accountability it will continue to cooperate with Western countries.
A key feature of the BNP’s vision for 2030 and its 2026 election manifesto is the party’s emphasis on “special relations” with Muslim countries for both ideological and practical reasons—namely, ensuring access to markets, remittance transfers from migrant workers in the Gulf states, and oil from Muslim-majority nations like Malaysia to stabilize the energy sector.[13] Another key aspect of the BNP’s manifesto is its focus on national security, including proposals to develop a national security council, a comprehensive national security strategy, and “credible deterrence” against threats.[14] Moreover, the BNP-led government has recently signed a free trade agreement with Japan, which is a major development partner, and has started negotiations with the European Union.[15] It appears that the BNP will maintain a balanced foreign policy approach, reminiscent of an emerging middle power striving to protect its strategic autonomy in an increasingly tumultuous world.
Finally, the BNP is unlikely to restore Bangladesh’s special relationship with India observed under Hasina’s Awami League–led government. BNP supporters are sensitive to the anti-Bangladesh sentiment that has become pervasive in India. Moreover, anti-Bangladesh rhetoric espoused by Indian politicians, particularly in border states, is not well received among Bangladesh’s populace. General disdain for the Awami League, and by extension its favored relationship with New Delhi, has soured prospects for a future return to the status quo in the bilateral relationship under a BNP-led government.
The BNP’s own foreign policy wing has been rushed through a generational shift as relatively young, dynamic, visionary, and suave personnel take over the party. After the BNP formed a government following the February 2026 elections, three of the most significant personnel handling international affairs who are currently in government are Humaiun Kobir, a state minister for foreign affairs; Shama Obaed Islam, also a state minister for foreign affairs; and Saimum Parvez, special assistant to the prime minister of Bangladesh on environment, forest, and climate change.[16] Several key themes are visible in regard to the BNP’s foreign policy.
A pragmatic approach to foreign policy. The BNP’s foreign policy approach reflects a shift from a traditional ideological approach to one with a greater focus on “national interest,” with “Bangladesh first” being the key slogan. For Parvez, approaches to foreign policy should be issue-based and contextual rather than holistic. In my interview with him, he highlighted that on certain issues there can be alignment, while on others there can be divergences with the same external actors. Rather than approaching foreign policy idiosyncratically, the BNP would approach every issue distinctly and contextually, with the attainment of national interest being the key.
Omnidirectional foreign policy. For the BNP, maintaining effective relations with all global powers is the key objective. Considering Bangladesh’s economic realities, Parvez emphasized the importance of maintaining good relations with major global actors. In particular, he stressed the need to have good and balanced relations with both the United States and China, without being drawn into a major geopolitical alliance. Rather than terming this approach to foreign policy as nonaligned, it might be described as “omnidirectional.”
India question. Parvez emphasized the need for equal and respectable bilateral relations with India. He mentioned the outreach by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and highlighted that the sheltering of Bangladeshi criminals in India has become a hurdle. Gufic Biosciences Limited (NSE:GUFICBIO) disclosed on 23 October 2026, under SEBI Listing Regulation 30, that the USFDA completed a Pre-Approval Inspection at the company's Indore, Madhya Pradesh manufacturing facility between 15 October and 23 October 2026, concluding with three observations issued in Form FDA 483.
Key Highlights
- The USFDA conducted a Pre-Approval Inspection at Gufic Biosciences' Pithampur, Indore facility from 15 October to 23 October 2026, spanning nine consecutive working days.
- Upon conclusion of the inspection, the company received exactly three observations recorded in Form FDA 483, which is a standard USFDA documentation mechanism for inspectional findings.
- Gufic Biosciences stated it will work closely with the USFDA and is committed to addressing all three observations comprehensively within the stipulated timeframe.
- The intimation was filed pursuant to Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and signed by Company Secretary Ami Shah.
About the Company
Gufic Biosciences Limited, listed on the NSE under ticker GUFICBIO and on BSE under scrip code 509079, is a Mumbai-headquartered Indian pharmaceutical company. It specialises in the manufacturing of lyophilised (freeze-dried) injectable formulations, critical care products, and fertility medications, serving both domestic and international markets. The company operates manufacturing infrastructure in Navsari, Gujarat, and Pithampur, Madhya Pradesh.
Announcement in Detail
According to the exchange filing dated 23 October 2026, the USFDA carried out a Pre-Approval Inspection at the company's manufacturing facility located at Plot No. 48, Smart Industrial Park, Near Natrip, Pithampur, District Dhar, Indore, Madhya Pradesh, pin code 454775. The inspection ran from 15 October 2026 to 23 October 2026. A Pre-Approval Inspection is initiated by the USFDA specifically to assess whether a manufacturing site is capable of producing a drug product in accordance with the conditions described in a pending new drug application or abbreviated new drug application before the agency grants market approval.
At the close of the inspection, the USFDA issued Form FDA 483, which is the standard document used by investigators to record observations of conditions or practices that, in their judgement, may constitute violations of applicable regulations. The filing confirms the company received three such observations. Gufic Biosciences stated that it remains committed to addressing these observations comprehensively within the timeframe stipulated by the USFDA, and that it will engage closely with the agency throughout this process.
Impact on Investors
Investors will note that a Form FDA 483 with three observations does not, by itself, constitute a Warning Letter or an import alert, and the USFDA's review of the company's written response is a standard next step in the pre-approval process. However, the filing shows that the outcome of this inspection directly affects the timeline for any product approval linked to the inspected facility. Shareholders will observe that delays in resolving the observations could extend the period before the company receives approval for the drug product associated with this Pre-Approval Inspection.
The disclosed terms indicate that no regulatory action beyond the Form 483 has been communicated as of the filing date. Investors will also note that Gufic Biosciences' ability to convert its US-directed pipeline into revenues depends, in part, on satisfactory closure of such inspectional observations to the USFDA's satisfaction, making the company's written response and subsequent USFDA communication material events to monitor.
Sector / Market Context
The Indian pharmaceutical industry is a significant supplier of generic medicines to the United States, and USFDA inspections of Indian manufacturing facilities have been a consistent regulatory feature for domestic drug makers seeking US market access. According to data compiled by the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India, pharmaceutical exports from India to the US remain among the largest bilateral trade flows in the sector, with pre-approval and surveillance inspections forming a routine part of the approval pathway for generic drug applications filed under the US Hatch-Waxman framework.

I would also like to emphasise that the maintenance of peace and tranquility in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations," he added.
Last week, the MEA had reiterated that the Union Territory of Ladakh remains an "integral and inalienable part of India" and no amount of denial by the Chinese side can change the fact.
Responding to media queries regarding comments made by the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson on Ladakh, the MEA spokesperson had referred to the Ministry of Home Affairs' statement, which mentioned that the 28 places in Ladakh have been identified with standard place and feature names on the official map of Survey of India. This, he asserted once again, has been done in consultation with the Union Territory of Ladakh and local stakeholders.
"It is reiterated that the UT of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India. No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact. As for the press release by the Ministry of Home Affairs, GOI, which is being referred to, it is self-explanatory. The announcement mentions that the twenty-eight (28) places/features located in the UT of Ladakh have been identified with standard place and feature names on the official map of Survey of India, and it has been done in consultation with the Union Territory of Ladakh and local stakeholders. Identifying these places formally on the Survey of India map of UT of Ladakh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large," he said.
The MEA's response came after Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning on October 13 opposed India's Ministry of Home Affairs identification of 28 places of Ladakh by standard place and names on the official map, terming it as "illegal and void."
Earlier this month, the Centre identified 28 places/locations in Ladakh by standard place and feature names on the official map of the Survey of India in order to recognise their geographical significance and for awareness of the general public about their exact location.
In September, External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar, during his visit to New York, said that India's relationship with China has improved from the depths of their border stand-off, but the condition of the frontier will continue to determine how far the two countries can normalise ties.
EAM Jaishankar said the India-China relationship was better than it had been in 2025, and better still compared with 2024. He cautioned against treating that recovery as a fundamental change in the relationship.
"I don't think it's structural change so much as a recovery from how far ties had deteriorated, he said. After the events of 2020 and the prolonged border stand-off, normal contact between the two countries had been severely affected.
Trade continued, but official exchanges, visas and flights were disrupted, he said. As the stand-off eased, some of those contacts began to return. EAM Jaishankar described that as a natural consequence of stabilisation rather than proof that the underlying issues had disappeared.
"A dip in our relationship actually doesn't help either of us," he said, adding that third parties could benefit from such a situation.
In September, Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, where the two leaders emphasised that "differences should not become disputes" and reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties.
During the meeting, PM Modi had stressed that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations.

articles.title: India’s Economic Security Begins In Its States - Outlook Business
articles.summary: India’s Economic Security Begins In Its States  Outlook Business
articles.full_text:
- Industrial concentration improves efficiency through specialised suppliers, skilled workers and established manufacturing ecosystems
- Japan’s semiconductor and automotive supply-chain disruptions demonstrate how infrastructure failures and dependence on critical suppliers can interrupt production
- India needs to assess strategic dependencies and balance the cost of alternative capacity against the economic consequences of supply-chain disruptions
In February 2024, the Union Cabinet approved India’s first commercial semiconductor fabrication plant to be developed at Dholera in Gujarat. Its success depends on reliable power, ultra-pure water, suitable land, skilled technicians and effective coordination among local agencies. By May 2026, twelve semiconductor projects involving proposed investments of approximately ₹1.64 lakh crore had been approved under the India Semiconductor Mission. In July, the Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0 with a budgetary outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. Every project must ultimately take shape in a particular district of a particular state. Where strategic production happens is not merely a matter of administrative detail but also an economic-security decision.
India’s economic-security debate operates largely at two levels. The Centre identifies strategic dependencies and finances incentives. Firms decide where to invest. Between them stands the state government, whose capabilities help determine whether investment becomes a functioning industrial ecosystem. Land and water are principally state responsibilities. Electricity is concurrent, but distribution is largely managed by state utilities and regulated by state commissions. A subsidy, by itself, cannot energise a substation or clear a disputed land title.
Three propositions follow. First, economic security is implemented geographically. National policy succeeds only where productive and institutional capabilities exist. Second, industrial strength is not resilience. Concentration generates efficiency but can also amplify exposure to local shocks. Third, India’s federal diversity can become a strategic asset. This is the principle of capability federalism.
Advertisement
Capability federalism means developing specialised productive capabilities across states while ensuring that strategically critical functions have credible alternatives through qualified suppliers, production locations and resilient infrastructure networks. Gujarat and Maharashtra illustrate the argument. They possess different industrial capabilities, although neither their strengths nor their differences establish national resilience.
Gujarat has emerged as the anchor of India’s semiconductor programme. Six of the twelve approved projects are located there, including the Tata–PSMC fabrication plant at Dholera and Micron’s assembly and testing facility at Sanand, which began operations in February 2026. The six projects represent approximately ₹1.28 lakh crore in proposed investment, nearly four-fifths of the national total. This is a concentration of investment commitments, not completed production capacity.
Advertisement
Gujarat combines industrial infrastructure, ports, chemical industries and substantial incentives. Its semiconductor policy provides capital assistance equivalent to 40% of eligible central assistance. The enduring test is whether these incentives create competitive supplier networks, skills and infrastructure.
Maharashtra brings a different depth. According to the Annual Survey of Industries 2024–25, it contributes 15.92% of India’s registered manufacturing gross value added, against Gujarat’s 14.10%. Maharashtra accounts for 13.08% of factory employment but 17.64% of factory emoluments, indicating higher average remuneration. Maharashtra's Pune, Chakan, Nashik and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar clusters have extensive engineering and supplier networks. Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority in Raigad handled 8.17 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) in 2025–26. The issue is not about which state is more successful. It is whether their different capabilities can contribute to a national production system that is both competitive and resilient.
Industrial clustering is often a sound policy choice. Since Alfred Marshall, economists have explained why firms gain from proximity through shared suppliers, specialised workers and the exchange of knowledge. A semiconductor fab cannot be recreated simply by allocating land elsewhere. Dispersing such facilities for regional symmetry could destroy the efficiencies that make them viable.
Yet concentration creates shared infrastructure vulnerabilities. On 12 October 2020, a cascading transmission failure blacked out Mumbai and surrounding areas, disrupting suburban rail services and forcing hospitals onto backup power. The episode demonstrated how failure at a critical infrastructure node can propagate across an advanced metropolitan economy.
Factories face similar dependencies. Geographically separated plants may rely on the same specialised equipment, chemicals, suppliers or logistics networks. The relevant distinction is between productive capacity, what a place can manufacture under normal conditions, and strategic resilience, what the wider economy can continue producing when a critical node fails. The obvious objection is cost. India is still developing its first commercial fab and cannot justify duplicating such investments merely for redundancy.
But some vulnerabilities can be addressed more economically. In semiconductor packaging, specialty gases, battery materials and mineral processing, alternative capacity may be developed at substantially lower cost than duplicating a fabrication plant. The objective is not maximum dispersion. It is the lowest-cost credible protection against strategically consequential disruption.
Japan demonstrates both industrial concentration and shared dependencies. Aichi and neighbouring Shizuoka have sophisticated manufacturing ecosystems through decades of investment in suppliers, skills and industrial institutions. In 2023, Aichi accounted for approximately 14.5 per cent of Japan's manufactured shipments, the highest among its prefectures. The 2011 earthquake halted Renesas’s Naka semiconductor plant in Ibaraki. Renesas then supplied roughly 40 per cent of the global automotive microcontroller market, making the disruption particularly consequential for international carmakers. In March 2022, a systems disruption at Toyota supplier Kojima Industries forced Toyota to suspend all 28 production lines at its 14 domestic plants for a day.
The incidents reveal different vulnerabilities: one involving physical disruption, the other a critical supplier dependency. Geographic dispersion alone cannot resolve either. Japan’s experience suggests that resilience requires understanding where critical functions are concentrated, how production networks are connected and how quickly disrupted capacity can be restored.
The India–Japan State–Prefecture Partnership Initiative launched in 2025 offers an opportunity to connect Indian states with Japanese industrial regions through technology, supplier development and skills. Such partnerships could deepen India’s productive capabilities while creating additional options for Japanese firms.
Capability federalism needs three instruments. First, industrial incentives must be linked to local infrastructure performance. Semicon 2.0’s implementation framework should evaluate power reliability, industrial water, logistics and administrative execution alongside project economics. Central support should be disbursed against verified infrastructure milestones. State utilities and infrastructure agencies should enter enforceable service-level agreements covering supply reliability, restoration times and independent backup arrangements.
Second, a National Strategic Production Resilience Assessment should be established, beginning with semiconductor packaging, battery materials, critical-mineral processing and essential pharmaceutical inputs. Firms receiving substantial public support should confidentially disclose material supply-chain dependencies and provide scenario-based estimates of two metrics developed by David Simchi-Levi and colleagues at MIT. Time-to-recover is how long disrupted capacity takes to resume production. Time-to-survive is how long downstream production can continue at an acceptable level without that capacity. Where recovery exceeds survival, policymakers should assess the strategic consequences and compare the costs of inventories, alternative suppliers, faster restoration and qualified capacity elsewhere.
Third, state incentives should be aligned with national resilience rather than subsidy competition. Semicon 2.0 should require transparent assessment of combined central and state support and discourage incentives that merely shift investment between locations. Instead of automatically rewarding higher capital subsidies, the Centre could offer targeted co-financing for critical suppliers establishing economically viable alternative capacity in locations with independent infrastructure and supply-chain risks. Alternative capacity should receive support only where measurable national resilience benefits justify its additional cost.
India does not need every state to manufacture everything. It needs a network of capable places which are specialised enough to compete, connected enough to complement one another and sufficiently adaptable to prevent local disruption from becoming national vulnerability. The plant may be announced in Delhi, but its resilience must be built in the states.
(This article is authored by Ashish Kumar Singh, IAS (Retd.), Distinguished Fellow, Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Views expressed are personal.)

articles.title: Tata Electronics wants bigger bite of Apple - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Tata Electronics wants bigger bite of Apple  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The company is seeking to climb the value chain and garner a larger piece of the Apple pie in India, an industry source said. This becomes significant as Tata Electronics is the fourth-largest Tata Group company by revenue and has emerged as a top-tier Apple supplier in the country.
“The company has scaled effectively for iPhone casings and is now looking to deepen its presence in the category,” said one of the people cited above. “It is assessing a foray into glass-based enclosures and a clutch of other metal parts and components that make up the category.”
Queries sent to Tata Electronics and Apple remained unanswered until the publication of this report. Analysts said this strategic diversification coincides with Apple’s India push. The country now reportedly assembles a quarter of worldwide iPhones and clocked a record $13.2 billion in iPhone exports in the first five months of this fiscal year.
Tata Electronics was among the players that received approval under the ECMS for the enclosure category. In fact, the bulk of the approved amount, ₹27,166 crore, was earmarked for three projects dedicated to mobile enclosure manufacturing by Tata Electronics, Motherson Group and Taiwanese major Foxconn’s India arm Yuzhan Technology.
Value chain
Tata Electronics’ proposed expansion into the broader enclosures category is being seen as a natural progression as it looks to broaden its expertise as an Apple supplier.
Neil Shah, co-founder and vice president - research at Counterpoint Research, explained the strategic importance of the enclosure. He said that in advanced electronics manufacturing such as premium smartphones from Apple or Samsung, an ‘enclosure’ is far more than a protective outer shell and is an intricately engineered multi-tier design to give form, function and fashionability.
“Understanding the enclosure means recognising that precision mechanical engineering is just as foundational to a smartphone’s performance as its silicon,” he said. “Tata Electronics looking to move into this complex CNC machining, structural metal parts, and glass integration is a natural leap up the value curve.”
Shah said that final assembly historically captures low single-digit margins, whereas precision mechanicals demand proprietary tooling, high capex, and superior yields that unlock much higher margin realisation.
“This is where players such as Foxconn, Luxshare, Huaqin, BYD and others have done pretty well,” he explained. “Assembling the outer chassis locally is what could transform India’s indigenous capability to become an advanced electronics manufacturing and assembly powerhouse with Tata at the forefront of the local EMS cohort.”
‘Formidable' partner
Further, with their component PLI backing, Shah said this vertical integration anchors the company as a formidable partner for Apple’s unanimous levelling diversification strategy.
Counterpoint’s Shah emphasised that Apple’s local partners in India have to move up the chain in investments, capability and experience curve to reach the level of craftsmanship Apple and their users expect, and enclosures are a great place to double down.
Prabhu Ram, vice president, industry research group, Cyber Media Research, too, backed the view that a move into glass-based enclosures and a wider range of metal components would build on Tata Electronics’ growing manufacturing maturity and recent growth momentum.
“Hosur already provides Tata Electronics with a base in precision machining, tooling and surface finishing for metal casings,” he said. “Expanding into adjacent components and materials could build on these capabilities, enabling the company to capture a greater share of component value and broaden its precision-manufacturing portfolio.”
He added that this would also signal a move up the value chain.
“If successful, the expansion could strengthen Tata Electronics’ position in the electronics manufacturing ecosystem, creating opportunities for deeper customer integration, greater engineering involvement and participation in more complex manufacturing programmes. It would also align with Apple’s broader push to deepen component manufacturing and value addition in India as it diversifies its global supply chain,” Ram said.

articles.title: Kharge demands Modi clarify India’s China policy amid tensions - The News Mill
articles.summary: Kharge demands Modi clarify India’s China policy amid tensions  The News Mill
articles.full_text:
Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge has called on Prime Minister Narendra Modi to provide clarity on India’s China policy, criticising the government’s handling of border security, economic ties, and diplomatic engagements.
In a post on X, Kharge directed three specific questions at the Prime Minister, covering national security, economic dependence, and diplomatic accountability. He highlighted remarks by the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General that confirmed ongoing face-offs with the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) in Arunachal Pradesh.
Kharge said, “The ITBP DG’s confirmation of continuing PLA face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh is deeply alarming. After Doklam and Galwan, is another serious confrontation unfolding? Reports of Chinese incursions near Taksing emerged in August. Yet, even 47 days after Corps Commander-level talks at Wacha–Damai, reportedly just 180 km away, confrontations continue. Has India’s patrolling access been compromised? Arunachal Pradesh is an inseparable part of India. Why is the nation being kept in the dark?”
He also expressed concern over India’s increasing trade deficit with China since the 2020 Galwan Valley clash. “Since the Galwan sacrifice of 20 Indian Army bravehearts (FY2020–21), Chinese imports have surged 102%, while India’s trade deficit with China has ballooned 155% to $112.16 billion. Even Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman admits China obstructs Indian exports. Yet, the Government is easing Chinese investment restrictions and considering Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) benefits for eligible China-linked ventures. Has Make in India become Import from China?”
Regarding diplomatic efforts, Kharge noted, “At least 23 reported Modi–Xi meetings and interactions, 25 Special Representatives’ rounds involving NSA Ajit Doval, 36 Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) meetings, and successive SCO and BRICS Summits. What tangible results have these engagements delivered? Have India’s pre-May 2020 patrolling rights been fully restored?”
He emphasised trust in the armed forces but criticised the government’s approach to diplomacy: “Our Armed Forces have our complete confidence. But National security demands accountability, not diplomatic photo opportunities & Hugplomacy! Instead of attacking the Opposition, PM Modi must take Parliament and the Nation into confidence.”
Earlier, Congress leader Pawan Khera accused the Centre of surrendering India’s interests to China, questioning the outcomes of its approach towards Beijing and whether Indian forces could still patrol pre-April 2020 areas.
At a press conference at the All India Congress Committee office in New Delhi, Khera questioned the government over border tensions, trade relations, visa policies, and the influx of Chinese workers, saying, “What did we get? What status did we get from anti? Can we patrol the points today where we used to patrol before April 2020, or not? In exchange for all this, shouldn’t you have taken something? Or did you just accept that little thing of theirs—that, sir, they will keep your secrets hidden, you will keep on crumbling, you will ruin the MSME of your country… you will do whatever China wants, because you are afraid of China. Just because you are afraid of China, you will keep surrendering India’s interests to China.”
He cited the rising trade deficit, increased visa allowances for Chinese workers, and easing travel restrictions, asking, “What does this do to India? What have we achieved out of this surrender?”
Khera rejected the government’s claims that the border situation was normal, citing social media posts from residents alleging Chinese incursions in Arunachal Pradesh. He added, “Every day you hear that China has entered Arunachal, people there are taking the help of social media, making emotional appeals there, local rural people… then our minister says, sir, I am swimming by jumping into the river, everything is normal here. What is this normal? This is not normal at all!”
He questioned whether there had been inquiries into the families of the 20 soldiers martyred in the Galwan clash and highlighted reports that China had blocked tunnel boring machines from reaching India via a German company, causing losses.
Khera remarked, “The strong country, the people of the country were with you—I was, I am deliberately saying, now I am not. The country’s soldier is brave, does not fear martyrdom; then why are you scared? That is why we say this secret won’t remain a secret for long. On the other hand, Epstein blackmails—gets blackmailed from Epstein’s files, so surrenders in front of America. Everywhere you are seen getting blackmailed. We kept whatever conditions they had; I put those terms in front of you. There is a tunnel boring machine, TBM. 70% of tunnel boring machines are made in China across the entire world. A German company was making tunnel boring machines; India had to buy them. China stopped its factory from sending them to India… unofficially, first of all, that, we won’t let tunnel boring machines go, stopped it, causing a loss to India.”
Congress MP Jairam Ramesh also criticised the government earlier, accusing it of making concessions to China and remaining silent over border tensions, claiming that India had lost patrolling points in Arunachal Pradesh.

articles.title: Strategic partnership between India and Poland should translate into joint ventures: PM Donald Tusk - Deccan Herald
articles.summary: Strategic partnership between India and Poland should translate into joint ventures: PM Donald Tusk  Deccan Herald
articles.full_text:
"Now it is time to translate these declarations into joint ventures," Tusk said, addressing the India-Poland Business Forum here. He called for greater technological cooperation between the two countries to strengthen their economies and help them access global markets.
PM Tusk highlighted the city's role as a global technology and innovation hub.
"This place (Bengaluru) shows how investing in people, knowledge, and entrepreneurship can change the position of the entire economy," he added.
Recalling that India and Poland elevated their ties to a strategic partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Warsaw in August 2024, Tusk said the action plan covered technological cooperation, cybersecurity and the space sector.
"Now it is time to translate these declarations into joint ventures," he said, adding that cooperation should strengthen both economies and help them compete in global markets.
On information technology and digitisation, the Polish leader proposed partnerships combining India's large IT services sector with his country's expertise in software, cloud solutions, automation and cybersecurity.
He said Polish companies could bring specialised solutions and European market experience, while Indian partners could help scale production and services.
Highlighting digital public services, he cited India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and Poland's electronic government services and mObywatel digital identity application as examples of expertise the countries could share.
"Together we can develop secure solutions that make everyday life easier for citizens and businesses," he said, stressing that digitalisation should improve productivity, reduce costs and enhance service quality.
Tusk said artificial intelligence (AI) should occupy a special place in bilateral cooperation, with opportunities to develop applications for industrial automation, data analysis, diagnostics and infrastructure management.
He also called for tools for small and medium-sized enterprises and greater cooperation between universities and research institutes in machine learning and data analysis.
"Cybersecurity, information protection, and digital infrastructure resilience are therefore both a common challenge and an area of new business opportunities," he said.
Identifying aerospace as the second major pillar of cooperation, PM Tusk cited India's Chandrayaan-3 mission, which landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023, and Poland's participation in the European Space Agency (ESA).
He said Polish companies and research centres had expertise in electronics, optical systems, software, scientific instruments and satellite-data analysis, and called for these complementary capabilities to be used jointly.
Tusk cited the participation of Polish astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski and Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla in the 2025 Axiom-4 mission to the International Space Station as a symbol of bilateral space cooperation.
"The participation of astronauts from our countries in one crew showed that Polish and Indian specialists can work in the most demanding technological environment," he said.
Polish space companies were already exploring Indian partnerships in satellite components, Earth observation, navigation software, data analytics, space security and dual-use solutions.
"If we can participate together in an international space mission, we should also develop specific industrial projects here on Earth," he said.
The Polish PM further said startups and research teams in both countries needed investors and access to customers. He recalled Poland's participation in the Bengaluru Tech Summit in 2025 and said the country would return for this year's edition in November.
He said he expected the forum to lead to new partnerships between ICT companies, jointly developed and exported AI solutions, opportunities for Polish companies to participate in Indian space programmes and initiatives to commercialise technology.
Public institutions, he said, should help entrepreneurs find partners, overcome barriers and secure project financing, declaring the Polish government's readiness to support cooperation.
"Let's not just use the technologies of the future; let's create them together and introduce them to global markets together," he said.

articles.title: Why The India-China Border Dispute Over Arunachal Pradesh Remains Unresolved - Outlook India
articles.summary: Why The India-China Border Dispute Over Arunachal Pradesh Remains Unresolved  Outlook India
articles.full_text:
- ITBP chief Shatrujeet Kapur has confirmed continuing face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at several locations along the Arunachal Pradesh frontier
- India’s decision to standardise the names of 27 geographical features in August prompted fresh objections from Beijing, which continues to claim the region as South Tibet
- The dispute remains unresolved because India recognises the McMahon Line as the basis of the eastern boundary, while China rejects it; diplomatic mechanisms have helped manage tensions but have not produced a final settlement
India-China tensions along the Arunachal Pradesh frontier have resurfaced after Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) chief Shatrujeet Kapur confirmed on Thursday that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops were continuing at several locations. The remarks followed reports of a stand-off in the Asaphila area since late July and came two months after Beijing objected to India’s formal naming of 27 geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh.
The dispute over the names reflects a deeper disagreement over sovereignty. India regards Arunachal Pradesh as an integral part of the country, while China calls the region “Zangnan”, or South Tibet, and rejects what it describes as India’s establishment of the state. Beijing said in August that India’s naming exercise was “illegal, null and void” and would not change its claim to the territory.
Neither the latest face-offs nor the competing naming exercises have resolved the underlying boundary question. Instead, they illustrate how the dispute continues to surface through military encounters, maps, official statements and infrastructure development, despite repeated efforts to manage tensions along the frontier.
Why Has The Dispute Resurfaced?
Kapur said on Thursday that confrontations had occurred at several locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border in the preceding days and were continuing. The ITBP chief also referred to the role of the force’s newly raised Shaurya commandos and called for greater investment in weapons modernisation, drones and counter-drone systems.
Separately, media reports citing government sources described a stand-off near Asaphila, close to Taksing, and reported that Chinese troops had pitched tents near Maja in Upper Subansiri district. Those specific accounts should be distinguished from Kapur’s broader public confirmation of continuing face-offs.
The military developments followed India’s August announcement that it had formally identified 27 geographical places and features in Arunachal Pradesh on Survey of India maps. The list included passes, land areas, a lake and a monument. The Ministry of Home Affairs said the exercise, undertaken with the state government, was intended to facilitate accurate identification and public awareness of the locations.
China responded three days later. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing did not recognise the state of Arunachal Pradesh and maintained that the region belonged to China. India rejected the objection, reiterating its position that the state was an integral part of the country.
The naming dispute is therefore part of a recurring contest over how the territory is represented and administered. Maps and place names can reinforce a government’s territorial position, but neither changes control on the ground nor resolves competing boundary claims.
What Is Behind China’s Claim?
The dispute centres on the McMahon Line, drawn during the 1914 Simla Convention involving representatives of British India, Tibet and China. Named after British Indian foreign secretary Henry McMahon, the line was intended to define the eastern section of the boundary between British India and Tibet.
India treats the McMahon Line as the basis of its boundary with China in the eastern sector. Beijing rejects it, arguing that Tibet did not have the authority to enter into such an agreement as an independent sovereign entity. China consequently claims parts of present-day Arunachal Pradesh, including Tawang, as part of what it calls South Tibet.
The disagreement reflects competing interpretations of the historical status of Tibet and the validity of the arrangements made during the colonial period. What India regards as an established boundary, China considers an outcome of an agreement it does not recognise.
This is part of a wider boundary dispute that extends beyond Arunachal Pradesh. India and China have competing claims in the western sector, including Aksai Chin in Ladakh, while differences over the alignment of the Line of Actual Control (LAC) have contributed to confrontations elsewhere along the frontier.
The LAC is the line separating areas under Indian and Chinese control, but its alignment has not been mutually delineated across the entire boundary. Differing perceptions of where it runs can bring patrols from both sides into the same areas, creating opportunities for face-offs even without either government announcing a change to its territorial claim. The eastern sector remains one of the most sensitive parts of this unresolved dispute.
How Did NEFA Become Arunachal Pradesh?
Arunachal Pradesh’s administrative history is central to understanding why India rejects China’s claim. The region was administered as the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) before it was made a Union Territory and renamed Arunachal Pradesh on January 20, 1972. It became a full-fledged state on February 20, 1987, and has since remained under Indian administration.
Covering nearly 84,000 sq km, Arunachal Pradesh is the largest state in Northeast India by area. Its international borders extend along Bhutan to the west, Tibet to the north and northeast, and Myanmar to the east. The state’s mountainous terrain and river valleys have shaped both settlement and connectivity across the region.
For India, the state’s administration, elections, public institutions and integration into the Union reinforce its position that Arunachal Pradesh is Indian territory. China’s rejection of the state’s name and its claim over the region reflect a different position on sovereignty.
The two governments’ competing claims have not been reconciled by the passage of time or by Arunachal Pradesh’s formal statehood. India’s administrative control and China’s territorial claim continue to coexist as opposing positions, which is why developments such as map updates and official naming exercises can trigger diplomatic protests.
Why Does Tawang Matter?
Tawang is important to the dispute because of its location, history and cultural links with Tibetan Buddhism. Situated in western Arunachal Pradesh near the disputed frontier, it is home to the Tawang Monastery, a major centre of Tibetan Buddhist learning.
The monastery is also associated with the Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, who was born in the region. These religious and historical connections make Tawang significant in discussions about the relationship between Tibet and the eastern Himalayas. The Indian government has highlighted its cultural heritage as part of Arunachal Pradesh’s place within the country.
China’s claim to Tawang is connected to its broader argument that parts of Arunachal Pradesh historically belonged to Tibet. India rejects that claim and maintains that the boundary established by the McMahon Line places Tawang within Indian territory.
Historical and religious connections do not, by themselves, settle modern questions of sovereignty. Their importance lies in how they feature in the competing national narratives surrounding the region. Tawang’s position close to the frontier also gives it direct significance for border security and access through the eastern Himalayas.
The area has seen military confrontations before, including the December 2022 clash between Indian and Chinese troops near Yangtse. Such incidents demonstrate how the unresolved boundary question can shift from diplomatic exchanges to face-offs between patrols on the ground.
Why Does The Geography Matter?
Arunachal Pradesh’s geography gives the boundary dispute a strategic dimension beyond competing historical claims. Its high mountains, steep valleys and remote settlements make roads and logistical support important for both civilian administration and military deployment. Access to frontier areas can be difficult, particularly during adverse weather, making reliable connectivity a central concern.
India has expanded road and tunnel infrastructure in the region. The Sela Tunnel, built by the Border Roads Organisation on the Tezpur–Tawang route at an altitude of around 13,000 feet, provides all-weather connectivity and is intended to improve access to the border region. The project has both civilian and defence significance because it reduces reliance on mountain routes affected by weather.
The proposed Frontier Highway, or NH-913, illustrates the scale of the wider effort. According to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, the road has a planned length of 1,824 km along the Indo-Tibet-Myanmar border. Work on some stretches had already been taken up, while the remaining length was being sanctioned or awarded in multiple packages. It should therefore be understood as a project under implementation, not a completed highway.
Improved connectivity can support border villages, facilitate access to public services and strengthen the movement of personnel and supplies. But infrastructure also operates within the context of a contested frontier, where both sides monitor one another’s activity and seek to maintain their positions.
Myanmar adds a wider regional dimension because Arunachal Pradesh’s eastern border forms part of India’s broader Northeast frontier. Border management, connectivity and security in the region matter to India’s overall approach to its eastern neighbourhood. They do not, however, explain the origins of China’s claim to Arunachal Pradesh, which is rooted primarily in the disputed eastern boundary and the history of Tibet.
